articles.title: Endurance Energy hits a brief milestone in its quest for undersea geothermal power
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Endurance Energy says its prototype marine geothermal power system generated more electricity than it consumed during a recent deployment 300 miles off the Oregon coast — though the milestone lasted just 8.7 seconds.

The Seattle-based startup landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent releasing water at about 538 degrees Fahrenheit. The team operated the system remotely through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed.
The expedition marked Endurance’s fifth deployment to the ocean floor where it tested Adélie — a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin.

The company is part of a broader race to harness geothermal energy, using heat from water or steam under the Earth’s crust, converted into electricity. But while companies such as Fervo and Sage Geosystems focus on terrestrial sites, Endurance is the first commercial venture pursuing undersea sources.
“The main question we had is can the system generate more power than it uses,” Andrew Redd , Endurance’s founder and CEO, said in a statement about the expedition, which began last month.
“Adélie did,” he added. “Goddard’s first liquid-fueled rocket flew for two and a half seconds. Our first net-positive run lasted about nine. Our approach is to make it exist, then make it good.”
The test produced only a brief burst of surplus electricity, reaching a peak net output of 16.5 kilowatts. Challenges with the technology and a failure of a power cable cut the dive short.

The team also drilled what it called the world’s first geothermal well. At a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface, its machinery created two bore holes that tapped into hydrothermal fluid. It capped one hole and drilled a roughly 2-inch wide, 52-foot deep geothermal well at the other. While the well delivered hot fluid, it wasn’t suited for testing the energy system, sending the team to the natural vent.

Endurance said the expedition included voluntary environmental monitoring. The team mapped the seafloor to select the least disruptive test site, sampled water before and after operations, surveyed marine life and monitored sound.

While the startup has made rapid progress, its approach faces significant challenges: high pressure and corrosive conditions, mineral buildup inside equipment and the risk of costly repairs to seafloor machinery. And although many population centers sit near coastlines, the systems would still need expensive subsea cables to carry electricity over potentially long distances.
The company has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three-dozen employees.
This winter, Endurance plans to deploy Gentoo, a refurbished and upgraded version of Adélie designed to generate more power for longer periods.
The company is also developing its first commercial project in Tonga, with the goal of delivering its first electricity in 2027.

articles.title: Portal Space Systems reaches orbit for the second time this year with Starburst-1 launch
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Portal Space Systems has reached Earth orbit for the second time this year, successfully launching the startup’s first free-flying spacecraft, Starburst-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

Portal’s Starburst-1 lifted off Tuesday at 7:04 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. The spacecraft separated from SpaceX’s Falcon 9 on the Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission about 57 minutes later.

Within hours of deployment, the Bothell, Wash.-based company reported that the desk-sized craft had established ground communications, stabilized itself, and successfully deployed its solar array to become power positive.

It marks the second significant milestone for Portal this year, following the March debut of Mini-Nova — a tissue-box-sized technology demonstration payload that flew on a SpaceX Falcon 9 mission to test critical control and power systems in orbit.

Portal self-funded Starburst-1 to accelerate its flight timeline and prove out hardware for prospective customers, achieving orbit in less than a year since introducing the Starburst vehicle concept in November 2025.
Co-founder and CEO Jeff Thornburg emphasized that urgency is baked into the startup’s operational philosophy, noting that customers require spacecraft that can shift rapidly in orbit.

“Speed can’t just be part of the product. It has to be part of the company building it,” Thornburg said in a statement. “Our customers need spacecraft that move quickly in orbit and a company that moves with the same urgency to get them there. We put our own capital behind Starburst-1 because proving hardware in flight is how we earn their confidence.”
Thornburg shared video of the launch and deployment of Starburst-1 on LinkedIn.

Starburst is an ESPA-class spacecraft designed to execute rapid maneuvers within a specific orbital regime, giving commercial and defense operators greater operational flexibility. The vehicle shares the majority of its core systems and manufacturing processes with Supernova, Portal’s larger upcoming spacecraft built for rapid travel across different orbital regimes, with flight data from Starburst-1 directly informing both platforms.
Starburst-1 is carrying experimental technologies from three partner companies to test in orbit:

Since emerging from stealth in 2024, Portal has raised $75 million in funding — including a $50 million round in April — from investors including Geodesic Capital, Mach33, Booz Allen Ventures, AlleyCorp, and FUSE, alongside receiving critical SBIR and STRATFI support from the U.S. military.

GeekWire got an inside look at Portal’s 8,000-square-foot Bothell development and testing lab earlier this year. To prepare for future demand — including a dedicated 2028 Falcon 9 mission known as Motus Via Sol that will carry multiple Starburst spacecraft and the first Supernova — Portal has been expanding its footprint.

The company is in the process of transitioning its satellite manufacturing operations into a new 65,000-square-foot facility in Bothell, which is slated to be fully operational by next year and capable of producing up to 16 Starburst and 12 Supernova spacecraft annually.

articles.title: UW protein institute led by Nobel winner unveils its first AI model co-developed with Nvidia
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: The UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design (IPD) today released a new open-source model for creating proteins with specific functions, called RFD4-Proteina. It is the first AI protein model the University of Washington has co-developed with semiconductor giant Nvidia.

The release comes on the heels of a major computing boost. Earlier this month, IPD announced it had received a large grant of computing power from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, through their foundation. In June, the institute began accessing Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, through cloud company CoreWeave. The grant is expected to support the institute for a year.

“RFD4-Proteina will open the door to new solutions in medicine, sustainability, materials and biotechnology,” David Baker, director of IPD and a 2024 Nobel laureate in chemistry, said in a statement. He earlier told GeekWire that the foundation’s grant has been “transformational” for the institute’s work.

IPD has used deep learning to develop and release a series of tools, including RoseTTAFold for predicting protein structures and RFdiffusion (RFD) for designing new proteins. The new model’s name nods to RFD and references Nvidia’s Proteina-Complexa computational models.
The team is touting RFD4-Proteina as “a considerable improvement over previous methods” that is faster and requires significantly less computational power.

The models have allowed researchers to design proteins never imagined before, with potential as drugs for challenging diseases or as tools for managing environmental waste such as toxic chemicals and plastics, among other applications. The IPD lists 11 spinout companies, including vaccine developer Icosavax and protein-design startup Archon Biosciences.

Seth Woodbury used RFD4-Proteina in his enzyme work as a , a UW bioengineering predoctoral candidate. “In just a few days we designed a pesticide-degrading enzyme that performs many fold better than my previous best, which took months to design,” he said. Woodbury last year published a paper in Nature on enzyme research.
At IPD, the RFD4-Proteina work was led by UW doctoral students Nathaniel Corley, Maxwell Kazman and Rafi Brent, along with Kieran Didi, a visiting student from the University of Oxford.
RFD4-Proteina is available through Berkeley Software Distribution.

articles.title: New fuel, same planes: Inside the bid to clean up air travel with cooking oil and captured carbon
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Subscribe to Positive Charge : Apple Podcasts , Spotify , Amazon Music , All Episodes

Taylor Swift was pilloried online over the climate impacts of her private jet travel for the Eras Tour and to see Travis Kelce, now her husband, play in the 2024 Super Bowl. Her representatives said she paid to offset the tour-related emissions, but the uproar highlighted a bigger problem: Aviation is a serious source of carbon dioxide, and it’s tough to fix.
Flying accounts for roughly 2.5% of global carbon dioxide emissions, and that share is expected to rise as other sectors adopt cleaner power.

The trouble is that jet fuel is so good at what it does. It holds enough energy to fly a plane nonstop from New York to Singapore. Cleaners sources likes batteries can’t begin to match that range, and hydrogen fuel faces hurdles including fuel storage and transfer and the need for aircraft redesigns.
That leaves aviation with one top alternative for today: sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF.

Instead of pumping more oil from underground, SAF uses carbon already on the earth’s surface. Manufacturers — including two in the American West — are making the fuel from sources such as cooking oil, animal fats, oil-rich plants, farm and forestry waste, or even captured carbon.

“SAF really fits a need that we have today and long into the future,” said Ryan Spies , managing director of sustainability at Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines . “SAF is the answer because it’s a drop-in fuel. That means we don’t have to change our planes, we don’t have to change what’s happening at the airport.”
The fuel remains in limited supply and use — only 1% of Alaska Air Group’s fuel is SAF, for example — but efforts are underway to expand production and adoption worldwide.
In tumbleweed country in central Washington, a startup called Twelve opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF from captured carbon dioxide this summer.

The site sits in an industrial stretch of Moses Lake in a largely agricultural area. Its neighbors include a fertilizer producer and battery materials manufacturer Sila. Low-cost, carbon-free hydropower has drawn businesses to the region, though data centers are creating competition for the energy.

To manufacture SAF, Twelve takes delivery of carbon dioxide that’s captured as a byproduct of ethanol production. The greenhouse gas is stored in a giant white tank. From there it’s pumped through insulated silver pipes that carry it through devices that remove oxygen and add hydrogen taken from water, producing the hydrocarbons that serve as fuel. The largely outdoor facility is shiny and new, with equipment stretching skyward.
The startup’s technology can make a variety of low-carbon products, including naphtha, a plastics precursor also produced at AirPlant One.
The site is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF, which is branded as E-Jet. The company is ramping up to that volume, said Nicholas Flanders , CEO and co-founder of Twelve.

“Even when we’re at that full capacity, there’s a lot more customer demand than we can make at AirPlant One,” he said. AirPlant Two, a much bigger facility that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is already in development. Flanders did not provide a timeline or location for the site.

About seven hours east of Moses Lake by car, Montana Renewables is producing SAF with a different approach. It makes the fuel at a century-old oil refinery that has been partially converted to renewable fuel and naphtha production.
“That’s the most economical way to to produce renewable fuels like SAF,” said Matt Upmeyer , vice president of commercial for Montana Renewables .
The facility uses feedstocks including used cooking oil, beef tallow from rendering plants and camelina, a lesser-known cover crop that helps farmers restore soil and also produces an oily seed.
Montana Renewables began making SAF in 2023, and by the next year was the largest SAF producer in North America, Upmeyer said, “which is a pretty cool stat.”
The company can produce 60 million gallons of SAF a year in Great Falls, Mont., and aims to reach 200 million gallons by the end of 2028.

That growth is significant, but the need is much higher. The U.S. government set a goal a few years ago of producing 3 billion gallons of SAF annually by 2030. A recent academic study involving researchers at Washington State University estimates the country could potentially reach 2.1 billion gallons by then. That total counts SAF from all U.S. producers, including Phillips 66, World Energy, Neste and LanzaJet.
By comparison, U.S. airlines use about 20 billion gallons of fuel a year, and that number is rising.

Cost is arguably the biggest hurdle to SAF adoption. The fuel is more expensive than traditional jet fuel, but the gap fluctuates because geopolitics moves oil prices. It should get cheaper as production scales, though demand will remain high.

Spies offered rough estimates for price comparisons. SAF made from fats, oils and greases — the most common form today — trades at less than double the price of jet fuel, he said. SAF from captured carbon, like Twelve’s, has the greatest environmental benefit, Spies said, but is “multiple times more expensive.”

Policy can help close the gap. The U.S. has used “carrots” such as a tax credit of up to $1.75 per gallon, created in 2022, but that was cut to $1 with President Trump’s return to office. Europe has opted for “sticks”: a requirement that 2% of jet fuel be SAF starting last year, which rose to 3.6% in the United Kingdom this year.

Customers are signing fuel purchase agreements, which can lock in prices and create demand that encourages more production. Alaska Airlines and Microsoft partnered with Twelve in 2022 to support its fuel’s development and use, helping create demand for the Moses Lake plant’s output.
Getting customers to sign these long-term deals “is really important for securing project financing,” Flanders said.

While SAF is the best near-term fuel for reining in aviation emissions, it still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere.

And there are other strategies for curbing aviation’s impacts that can compliment SAF, including designing more efficient planes, preventing contrail formation, and using flight plans that reduce emissions.

Most SAF produced today provides an 80% reduction . By Twelve’s calculations, if a plane used straight E-Jet, it could slash the flight’s carbon emissions up to 90% compared with jet fuel (there are some carbon costs for production and transportation).
Twelve’s Flanders put the benefits in perspective.

“To have 90% lower emissions when you fly, that would mean taking a domestic flight would have the same emissions per passenger mile as taking the London Tube,” he said. With flying on par with taking the train, “it really can change the impact of aviation on the environment.

articles.title: ‘Difficult relationship’: UW task force proposes splitting Allen School from College of Engineering
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: University of Washington leaders are weighing whether to separate the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering from the broader College of Engineering, after a task force recommended the move as part of proposed changes to UW’s computing and AI programs.
The split would give new independence to what has become one of the world’s leading schools for computer science and AI, and a major source of talent for the Seattle region’s tech industry.

As an independent, college-level school, the Allen School would gain greater control over its finances and a seat at the table with UW’s other deans. It could also put more of its own revenue toward teaching, as student demand for computing courses continues to outstrip its capacity .

The task force’s report , released this week, concluded that UW’s successes in computing, data science and AI have come “not because of the organizational structures we have in place but in spite of them.” The nine-member group included UW faculty leaders from across campus, two outside academics and an Amazon executive.
The report also described a “difficult relationship” between the Allen School and the College of Engineering, and “significant distrust” across campus over resources and priorities.
UW Engineering Dean Nancy Allbritton, in a statement to GeekWire on Tuesday, called the relationship “complex rather than difficult.”

The College of Engineering supports the university’s decision to “carefully evaluate” the task force’s recommendations, Allbritton said. She praised the Allen School and said the school and college share a long history of working together, with a commitment to students, research and service to Washington state.

The stakes extend well beyond university politics: The Allen School’s graduates are in high demand across the tech industry. Nearly 100 graduates from the 2025-26 class went to work full time at Amazon, and more than 70 went to Google, Microsoft or Meta, according to a survey of recent graduates by the school. In all, graduates went to more than 150 different companies.

No decision yet: UW President Robert J. Jones and Provost Tricia Serio said Monday that they aren’t making a decision yet. In a letter to the UW community , they announced two implementation committees.

Both committees are due to report by the end of winter quarter 2027, and UW leaders plan to announce next steps in spring 2027. Any changes would still need approval through the university’s usual processes, including the Faculty Senate and Board of Regents, with a goal of putting them in place by the end of the 2027-28 academic year.

The task force was co-chaired by Andy Connolly of UW’s eScience Institute and Kathy Yelick of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Its other members were Dan Grossman, now the Allen School’s interim director; Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau of the University of Wisconsin; UW’s Elizabeth Nance (chemical engineering), Abel Rodriguez (statistics), Emma Spiro (Information School) and Peter Tarczy-Hornoch (UW Medicine); and Anne Szeto of Amazon.

Allen School faculty voted 83-0 in late September in support of “moving forward with a process to determine how the Allen School would become an independent school,” with 13 not voting because they were absent or on leave, according to the school. A formal decision and vote would follow that process, the school said.

Budget and a seat at the table: The issue comes down to money and influence. UW’s budget model sends tuition and a share of research grant funding to the college where the courses are taught and the research is based.

For the Allen School, that’s the College of Engineering. As an independent school, the Allen School would control those funds directly, and its leader would sit with UW’s other deans when the university sets strategy on AI and other priorities, a voice the task force says computing has largely lacked.

UW’s Information School already operates as an independent, college-level unit. But the report says its focus on the human, societal and organizational side of computing and information is different from the Allen School’s focus on computing as a discipline.

As an initial step, Jones and Serio invited Grossman to participate in the Board of Deans and Chancellors. The letter says the move is “independent of any future decision about administrative structure.”

In a message to the Allen School community, Grossman called the invitation “a reflection of the Allen School’s scale and reach,” adding, “I’m pleased to have this opportunity to make meaningful contributions to discussions among UW’s leaders.”
He described the task force’s proposals as “exciting recommendations that will be great for the whole of UW and its impact on Washington state and beyond.”
Grossman also said there are “no planned changes to the Allen School’s structure, staffing, budget, policies and procedures, or degree programs” while the committees do their work.

A longtime Allen School professor and its former vice director, Grossman was named interim director this summer when Magdalena Balazinska’s nearly seven-year term as director ended. At the time, UW said it was opting for an interim leader for about a year while it weighed the task force’s recommendations, which hadn’t yet been made public.

The board seat was one of several early steps the task force recommended to show that UW was committed to the process. The task force also suggested having the Allen School’s director report jointly to the provost and giving the school more control over its budget, but UW hasn’t taken those steps for now.
Rooted in Paul Allen’s gift: The prospect of independence goes back to the Allen School’s creation in 2017.

When a $40 million gift from Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen turned UW’s longtime computer science department into the Allen School, the gift agreement said the school would “remain a unit of the College of Engineering, at least for the time being,” according to a copy obtained by GeekWire.

The agreement called for the school to receive the same prominence, visibility, support and privileges as UW’s other schools and colleges “to the greatest extent possible,” and anticipated that it could someday become “a free-standing School or College.”

The agreement also spelled out what would happen to the name if the school were ever “elevated to a College of the University”: it would change to reflect the new structure, but would “always prominently include” Allen’s name.

Impact on Engineering: The College of Engineering would lose its largest unit. The Allen School, which awarded 894 of the college’s 3,132 degrees in 2025-26, accounts for a little more than a quarter of the college by degrees, enrollment and faculty, according to figures from the college.
The report acknowledges “significant short- and long-term financial implications” from a separation and suggests options such as permanent financial support for Engineering to offset the loss.

Allbritton said the college is committed to helping shape an outcome that “strengthens the College of Engineering, strengthens computer science as an independent discipline, and advances the University of Washington’s broader mission of innovation, discovery, economic opportunity and public impact.”

The Allen School “is an extraordinary unit that has experienced remarkable growth and operates at a scale unlike any other department in the College,” she said. “As both organizations have evolved, there have naturally been questions about structure, governance, and how best to support future growth.”

She also noted that the College of Engineering has nearly doubled in size over the past decade “amid increasingly constrained public resources,” and said the college’s focus is on ensuring that students, faculty, staff, research partnerships and industry relationships “continue to thrive.”
“What has remained constant is a shared commitment to student success, research excellence and service to Washington state,” Allbritton said.

The report doesn’t detail the friction between the Allen School and Engineering. It says independence “does not directly address concerns voiced about collegiality” but could remove “a structural asymmetry that has complicated those relationships.” Opinion across campus on Allen’s independence was “genuinely divided,” the report says.

The federation’s role: The proposed federation is partly a way to keep the rest of campus on board. Other units worried that the Allen School would win independence while the federation never got real resources, according to the report, which recommends that the split not be finalized until the federation is up and running.
Much of the “distrust” cited in the report centers on whether one recommendation would advance at the expense of the other.
If the Allen School’s separation is finalized first, the report says, “other stakeholders are unlikely to trust that the federation will ever achieve the size and stature it needs.”

If the federation moves ahead without a clear commitment to independence, the Allen School and its supporters “are unlikely to trust that their important contributions toward the federation’s success will achieve meaningful change.”
The Allen School is already helping lead cross-campus efforts, including a new AI minor for students in all majors, developed with 18 academic units and set to launch in spring 2027.

Toward a college of computing: Other top universities have taken similar paths. Carnegie Mellon and Georgia Tech run computer science as standalone, college-level schools, while MIT, UC Berkeley and Cornell have created broader colleges of computing, according to the report.

Peer institutions’ computing colleges were “frequently propelled by a transformational naming gift,” the report notes, as with MIT’s Schwarzman College of Computing and Cornell’s Bowers College of Computing and Information Science.

The report describes the federation as a possible “transitional phase” toward a full College of Computing at UW, which would house the Allen School alongside other units, and recommends revisiting that idea in about five years.

articles.title: Rinck Pushes Against Gender-Based Violence, Facing Budget Headwinds
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: In the middle of a Seattle budget season marked by councilmember complaints and hyperbole, Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck has stepped forward to announce her “Seattle Stands With Survivors, Every Step” campaign. While anti-survivor rhetoric continues to pervade the national news, the federal government under President Donald Trump is cutting key investments that have historically supported survivors of gender-based violence – and Rinck wants Seattle to step in to help fill the gaps.

“Every two minutes, someone in this country is sexually assaulted,” Rinck said to kick off her press conference on Wednesday. “We cannot be serious about public safety in this city without also being serious about gender-based violence.”

“I stand here as your Seattle City Council member representing the Office of Position 8 and as a survivor myself,” Rinck continued. “I know what it costs to say those words out loud, but I know what it means when someone believes you and when someone is there to walk alongside of you. Every survivor in Seattle deserves that.”

Rinck wants to make $8 million in investments for survivors of gender-based violence in the 2027-2028 biennial budget to stabilize and scale up programs in three key areas: accountability for abusers and justice for survivors, direct survivor services, and prevention.

Rinck will also introduce a Statement of Legislative Intent (SLI) in order to help guide the work around funding and supporting these services in her Human Services, Labor, & Economic Development committee next year.

At her press conference, Rinck was flanked by fellow Councilmembers Dionne Foster, Eddie Lin, and Bob Kettle, as well as Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans, King County Councilmember Jorge Barón, State Representative Darya Farivar, and current LD-37 candidate for the State House Jaelynn Scott. Also present were many of the service providers with whom Rinck has been consulting to better understand the current needs in order to develop her campaign.

Riddhi Mukopadhyay, the executive director at the Sexual Violence Law Center (SVLC), said the average number of legal problems a Seattle resident who has survived domestic violence or sexual assault will experience is 19.7.

“Survivors cannot rely on the criminal system alone. Justice denied shows up costing more and hurting more,” Mukopadhyay said. “That's why community programs and legal services like ours matter. It's the collaborative network here that quietly keeps people housed, safe, employed, and in school. We don't make the headlines, but we do make the difference.”

Rinck spoke of the Jeffrey Epstein survivors who have spent years fighting to be heard, the case of the Cornell Seven gang rape , and the comedian opening Saturday Night Live by calling women who wear shorts in the gym “whores.”
“Three stories, one clear message to survivors,” Rinck said. “We don't believe you. It doesn't matter. Our fear and pain is just a joke.”

Rinck also mentioned the woman who was raped by a fraternity member at the University of Washington in 2022, who recently filed a suit against the university for failing to protect her from a known offender.

“ I think that as we see the national news over the last several years, and we see the lack of accountability, the amount of corruption, and lack of consequence for this very significant and profound harm that survivors are experiencing, I think it's incredibly meaningful to have elected leaders and and local communities responding very unequivocally that this is not okay, and we need to actually make sure that survivors have resources and have support,” Amarinthia Torres, the co-executive director of the Coalition Ending Gender-Based Violence, told The Urbanist .
Feminist Soraya Chemaly linked the problem of pervasive campus rape directly to our society’s widespread patterns of impunity and lack of accountability.

“What I’m describing is [a] closed loop of institutional self-preservation, power, and elite freedom from accountability,” Chemaly wrote . “The mechanisms evident in cases of sexual violence — diffusing moral culpability and liability, protecting influential and powerful classes of people, forcing victims to absorb costs as individuals — are the same as those we see across corporate and political institutions that pervasively externalize the costs and violence required to maintain unaccountable power and a life with no limits for a few.”

In a period some people consider to be a backlash to the #MeToo movement, the news contains a litany of stories involving the Trump administration: the scandal of the Epstein files showing a web of power with a convicted child sex offender at its heart, the White House intervening on behalf of accused sex trafficker Andrew Tate, Russell Brand moderating a recent panel at a recent Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) summit right before going on trial for multiple allegations of rape and sexual assault, and Trump’s own civil liability for sexual abuse (a legal finding before he was elected to the presidency for the second time) as well as the scores of allegations of sexual misconduct.
Meanwhile, headlines decry the influence of the “manosphere” and its impact on violence rates against women and children.

Within this context, Trump’s administration has moved decisively in cutting financial support for survivors of gender-based violence, which is having impacts across the country and in Seattle specifically.

In addition to cutting social safety net programs like Medicaid and SNAP, which assist survivors in trying to rebuild their lives, H.R. 1 cut over $200 million from the Office on Violence Against Women as well as survivor-specific assistance within the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). In the last two years, there have also been cuts to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention funding for violence prevention research, Department of Justice (DoJ) cuts to funding and training for child sex trafficking investigations and an attempt to cease grant-giving to organizations involved in Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) work, and cuts to the Prison Rape Elimination Act.

In the wake of the Cornell gang rape investigation being re-opened, the Trump administration weakened the Title IX rules reverting to stricter guidelines for formal complaints and procedures and r emoving protections for LGBTQ+ students . Former President Joe Biden had strengthened these rules in 2024.

“It's important to note that many folks who disproportionately experience gender-based violence are marginalized and often erased people, and folks who are already under attack by other national policies right now,” Rinck told The Urbanist . “I'm thinking about immigrant women, women of color broadly, trans people, just to name a few.”

Rinck wanted to bring attention to the local impacts of the federal cuts, which include Aurora Commons reducing the service hours of its Safe, Healthy, Empowered (S.H.E.) Clinic, Salvation Army and New Beginnings anticipating major cuts to domestic violence transitional housing, and ReWA dealing with federal funding cuts to legal assistance and housing services for refugee and immigrant survivors. Some organizations are opting out of all DOJ grants due to the concern about possible restrictions around DEI values.

“We really see the root causes of gender-based violence being about rigid gender and gender inequity, so abuses of power and disparity,” Torres said. “And I think that those root causes are really important to name as we think about how we address harm when harm happens and when violence happens because the folks that are the most vulnerable, that are the most marginalized, that are the most objectified, that is when violence is occurring, is to those folks that are most on the margins and where we see dehumanization and objectification occurring.”

Organizations serving transgender people are seeing lessened philanthropic support, meaning fewer resources for transgender people who have survived gender-based violence. The ability for organizations to serve unaccompanied immigrant children who are often victims of gender-based violence has dramatically diminished. Immigrants who are survivors are afraid that if they share about their abuse or try to get help, they might be deported, Torres said.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson’s 2027 budget proposal ends some one-time investments in this space, including $500,000 for gender-based violence services and $400,000 for commercial sexual exploitation work, as well as a $285,000 cut to the Office of Civil Rights program providing funding for community-led domestic violence response and prevention programs. These are some of the investments Rinck is looking to restore.
Rinck told The Urbanist she’s also looking to restore federal cuts to help stabilize programs and to help programs improve their staffing ratios.

Separate from Rinck’s $8 million plan, Foster will be introducing an amendment for a one-time budget add of $1 million to help address the Seattle City Attorney’s Office’s backlog of domestic violence and other cases. Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans shared that of the 5,000 case backlog inherited from her predecessor Ann Davison, 1,700 of them are domestic violence cases, referencing a recent case that had taken almost two years to be filed.

Seattle’s October revenue forecast , delivered last Friday, was not as rosy as some councilmembers might have hoped. From 2026-2028, the forecast predicted only $8.8 million in total additional revenues, meaning the city council will have very little wiggle room to fund their priorities in the current budget proposal without also implementing cuts.

“I would consider this a bad forecast, even though it could be much worse. This is one of the smallest increases in the last several years,” Budget Chair Dan Strauss told The Urbanist . “We are being asked to do more with less. The federal government continues to try and defund basic services, from SNAP benefits to permanent supportive housing. While we received a very small revenue increase in this forecast, Seattle is also being forced to take on more financial responsibility for doing the federal government’s job.”

Councilmember Bob Kettle has been vocal in criticizing Wilson’s budget proposal, particularly as it pertains to public safety: primarily the Seattle Police Department (SPD) and the Seattle Fire Department (SFD). Kettle has expressed particular concern over the plateau – at 1,250 officers – in SPD staffing that would occur at the end of next year, given that he believes the City requires 1,400 officers or more.
Some councilmembers also expressed concern that more money wasn’t being invested in the Unified Care Team that performs sweeps of unhoused people around the City.

Given the budget crunch, it is unclear if Kettle would have the votes to further fund a police department that is already receiving a larger increase in investment than any other City department under Wilson’s proposal. There does seem to be a stronger consensus amongst councilmembers to try to reverse the $7.1 million cut to SFD’s overtime budget.

A spokesperson from SFD clarified to The Urbanist that the unit outages it experienced in 2025 were unplanned, as opposed to the planned outages that would be taking place under the overtime restriction in 2027.

“As a result of unplanned unit outages in 2025, the department reinvested some of that funding in areas that surpassed their planned budget, including workers compensation (as a result of personnel injuries), minor equipment costs (as a result of inflation), and fleet maintenance and repair,” the SFD spokesperson said.
Last week, Central Staff member Ann Gorman told the council the unplanned 2025 SFD unit outages didn’t appear to impact response times.

The almost-flat budget forecast might not bode well for Rinck to be able to garner enough support from her colleagues to add $8 million in funding over the next two years for gender-based violence programs. Rinck assured The Urbanist she intends to fight for the investment, but she sees the campaign as a multi-year effort that will also involve work within her committee.

“We're daylighting this issue because we need to talk about gender-based violence,” Rinck said. “Far too many of the messages that women in the U.S. have gotten in the past week – past two weeks, past year, if I'm being honest – have been that gender-based violence and forms of sexual violence attached to that: people who perpetuate that will not be held accountable, or that people don't care, or that this is just a joke. And I think it's tremendously important that people in positions of power right now send a different message that we're actually not going to tolerate that, and we are going to hold you accountable.”
“Everybody knows a survivor of gender-based violence,” Torres said.

articles.title: Land use review underway for Broadway Crisis Center overhaul
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A key land use process has begun as officials aim for a planned end of 2027 opening of the Central Crisis Care Center emergency mental health facility on Broadway.

The Master Use Permit application for the 1110 Harvard Ave medical facility marks an important regulatory milestone in King County’s $56 million push to transform the three-story former Polyclinic building.
“The Project consist of the renovate an existing building into an acute behavior health care center,” the paperwork begins.

A Master Use Permit serves as the city’s official land-use gatekeeper, legally establishing changes in building use and occupancy before physical construction permits can be issued. According to project filings submitted on behalf of property owner King County, the renovation will convert the site into an acute behavioral health facility designed to maintain a “no wrong door’ approach” and an “open-door, 24/7 walk-in policy to serve all individuals who come to the center.”
Project plans call for interior and exterior upgrades that “apply the principles of trauma-informed design, and recognize the unique needs of individuals across the lifespan.”

The MUP also formalizes substantial exterior and access reconfigurations. it proposes eliminating 17 existing on-site parking stalls to rely on two proposed accessible on-street spaces, while managing more than 2,000 square feet of earth disturbance across public rights-of-way on Harvard, Broadway, and E Union as entrances to the facility are reconfigured.
The south end has been an empty lot for decades (Image: City of Seattle)
The plan does not specify any planned upgrades or use of the parcel’s empty southern portion long ago home to the Scottish Rite Cathedral .

Litigation and administrative appeals can delay or halt a Seattle Master Use Permit though the legal threshold required to substantially alter or kill a project is high. In most cases, litigation forces additional environmental studies, or extracts design concessions rather than outright stopping a permitted land use.
For renovation projects like 1110 Harvard Ave, standard building work without major exterior expansions or rezoning applications have limited targets for appeal.
On top of the $41.5 million acquisition cost of the building, officials have earmarked $11.5 million to $14.5 million in spending for renovation and operational start-up costs.
Recent filings also will enroll the property in the city’s Vacant Building Monitoring program as medical use of the building winds down.
This land use review intersects with neighborhood public safety efforts.

As the citizen-led Seattle Community Advisory Group formed to help shape planning for the project works to allocate a $3 million county mitigation fund to address street disorder and crime gaps, MUP filings dictate physical crime prevention through environmental design updates including sidewalk grading, frontage lighting, and secure access corridors.

CHS reported on the advisory group’s early work around public safety improvements focused heavily on surrounding street conditions. During an April session, members raised worries over “open-air drug markets, gun violence, property crime, and disorder,” warning that without strong post-crisis discharge planning, “people across King County could concentrate issues in Capitol and First Hill.”

CHS reported here on the 2025 approval of the $56 million plan to acquire the property, overhaul the building, and hire an operator for what is planned to be the second in a network of five county facilities providing 24-7 walk-in and emergency care mental health clinics funded by a 2023 voter-approved levy.
Last November , CHS reported on the selection of Connections Health Solutions to operate the center.
With officials targeting an opening in late 2027 now at the earliest, securing MUP approval is a critical step needed to clear contractor bidding and keep renovations on schedule.

articles.title: Seattle goes to court after ruling freezes plan for 6-story neighborhood centers along transit corridors
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: View the interactive map showing “Centers and Corridors” rezoning proposals here

The City of Seattle is launching a response to a state growth board ruling that has put plans on hold for new zoning for neighborhood centers and increased density along high-frequency transit corridors.

On September 9, the Central Puget Sound Growth Management Hearings Board upheld major elements of Seattle’s updated Comprehensive Plan including racial equity and water infrastructure but ruled its Environmental Impact Statement inadequate.
The matter was appealed to the board by anti-growth activists and conservation groups, including the Orca Conservancy, the Orca Network, and the Puget Sound Harvesters Association .

Under the State Environmental Policy Act and Growth Management Act appeal rules, petitioners can establish legal standing through organizational mission or geographic proximity. Membership total is not a factor.
The board directed the city to re-evaluate impacts using “maximum possible development” rather than standard 20-year growth estimates.
In response, Mayor Katie Wilson and City Attorney Erika Evans have challenged the ruling in court.
Meanwhile, the Office of Planning and Community Development began supplemental environmental analysis due by September 2027.

The decision has fully halted the Seattle City Council’s review of the Centers and Corridors legislation and the Downtown Regional Center Subarea Plan, slowing new housing expansions along transit routes.
CHS reported here on the Centers and Corridors plans and proposals that will bring renewed debate around future growth in areas like Montlake, Madison Valley, Madison Park, and Madrona.

The Centers and Corridors legislation “updates zoning in new growth areas identified in the Comprehensive plan, including: 30 new Neighborhood Centers, new and expanded Urban Centers, and transit corridors,” city officials say. The second phase of comprehensive updates focus on the 30 proposed Neighborhood Centers including Montlake, Madison Valley, Madison Park, and Madrona in the Capitol Hill area. The designation will “allow residential and mixed-use buildings up to six stories in the core and four and five-story residential buildings toward the edges,” according to one city summary. Once the neighborhood framework is in place, future Neighborhood Centers like Roanoke Park could be in play.

CHS reported here in December 2025 as the first phase of legislation setting the framework for the city’s new 20-year growth plan including state-mandated “Middle Housing” laws expanding zoning to allow a greater range of housing types in more parts of the city was finally wrapped up under leadership by District 3 representative Joy Hollingsworth .

“Every neighborhood should have housing choices for people across all incomes and backgrounds,” the city’s statement on the path to completing the second phase reads. “New residents should be able to settle in, longtime residents should be able to stay and thrive, working families should be able to comfortably raise their kids, and communities should be able to remain safe without fear of displacement.”
“Our land use policies and programs will support this vision,” it concludes.

articles.title: Seattle City Council Passes Draconian Effective RV Ban
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: Last night, the Seattle City Council passed the most comprehensive reform of large vehicle regulations in a generation to make it harder for homeless people to live in RVs and trailers. The six ordinances sponsored by Councilmember Dan Strauss will require people living in large vehicles to obtain a permit to park for more than two hours. Even with a permit, they’ll still have to move every 72 hours.

The legislative package aims to assuage longstanding complaints about sanitation and livability issues caused by RV residents in industrial neighborhoods while increasing outreach and services to the historically overlooked segment of Seattle’s homeless population.

However, many RV residents and homelessness advocates say the permitting system is a ban in disguise, and will just further hurt people already living on the margins, forcing them to either leave the city or get rid of what little property they still own.

The two most controversial bills in the legislative package, including the new permitting system, passed 6 to 3 at last night’s meeting, cleanly following the council’s ideological faultline. Mayor Katie Wilson hasn’t taken an official stance on the legislation, but expressed concerns about the costs of rolling out the new permitting system. If she chose to veto the bills, the council would have the votes to override it.

The Seattle bills mirror legislation recently passed by other municipalities like San Francisco, part of a nationwide crackdown on unsheltered homelessness in the wake of the 2024 Grants Pass decision.

While Strauss’s legislation is framed as a permitting system, it amounts to nothing less than a wholesale ban on RV living in Seattle, says Graham Pruss, executive director of the National Vehicle Residency Coalition.

The permitting system will only be available to people included in a one-time survey of vehicle residents. To obtain the permit, they’ll also have to maintain a valid vehicle registration—a significant hurdle for many—and ensure their RV or trailer is of habitable condition. Many homeless Seattleites live in dilapidated or rusty vehicles legally considered “junk” and ineligible for a permit.
Moreover, the permit won’t create a permanent legal status for RV dwellers; it can be revoked after six refusals of “appropriate” offers of shelter.
Strauss told The Stranger the phase out mechanism of the permitting system is by design—he doesn’t want Seattle to be seen as a destination for vehicle residents.
“If we were to leave the census open perpetually or forever, my fear is that we would have RVs coming from all of the Pacific Northwest, from Idaho to Oregon,” Strauss says.

In a letter to the council, the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness criticized the new permitting program and called on it to reject four out of the six bills. It said the funding for eight new staffers to enforce the permits was a bad use of taxpayer money and should instead go to direct outreach.

The coalition did support several aspects of Strauss’s proposal, including additional funding for outreach and the establishment of dedicated city-managed parking for RVs and trailers so that homeless residents entering shelter won’t have to get rid of their vehicles.

While a majority of homelessness service providers and advocates opposed the permitting system, the UHeights Vehicle Residency Outreach (VRO) came out in support of the legislation. VRO did not respond to a request for comment. Other supporters of the legislation, including a member of the Ballard Alliance and a representative of the North Lake neighbors group, testified in support of the legislation.

Pruss said that Strauss used promises of funding have been used as a “tool” to divide service providers and make the effective RV ban politically palatable. “For that funding, the rest of the folks who live in RVs in perpetuity are being banished from Seattle and the larger region of the Puget Sound,” he says.

Pruss warned that Seattle’s legislation will set off a wave of bans as RV residents get displaced outside city limits. That phenomenon has been playing out in the Bay Area, where a third of RV residents have already moved outside San Francisco since it passed its ban last summer.

Adding to the concerns is the lack of an active safe lot for vehicle residents within Seattle. The Low Income Housing Institute’s (LIHI) Salmon Bay safe lot was forced to close in May 2025 (it was turned into a pickleball facility). Safe lots make living in RVs easier, allowing residents to connect to power and sewage and be part of a stable community without the fear of being swept. LIHI plans to open its new Glassyard Commons site, serving 72 vehicles and 20 tiny houses, next month.
In her budget proposal, Wilson allocated funding for a second safe lot. Strauss says he is sponsoring a budget amendment to ensure that funding is included.

Even if both safe lots are operational, they won’t be able to serve all of Seattle’s RV residents. In this year’s Point-in-Time Count, UW researchers found that on any given night nearly 4,000 people are living in their vehicles across King County, including more than 600 in large vehicles such as RVs.
LIHI boasts that 60 percent of the 87 people who lived in the Salmon Bay safe lot eventually got permanent housing.

But for Tiffany Taylor, who is one of the 40 percent who didn’t end up with a home, Salmon Bay ended with bitter disappointment. While she appreciated the accommodations during her time in the safe lot, including the ability to keep her trailer, she had to get rid of it when Salmon Bay suddenly closed.

Instead of housing, LIHI offered her a place in one of its tiny houses. Taylor estimates that the trailer was worth about $9,000 when she moved into the safe lot. She says she was okay with the tradeoff as long as she ended up getting placed in an apartment.

However, earlier this summer, she got kicked out of her tiny house for having an unauthorized AC system, leaving her completely homeless once again. Taylor says that in order for the new RV permitting system to work, it will need to ensure people like her don’t fall through the cracks

“They need to do a better job of making sure that people are really taken care of and not just cycled out and left with nothing,” Taylor said. “Like now I’m just out there trying to figure it out all from ground zero.”

articles.title: Pop Loser: Bono Quoted Dan Savage
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! This week, unexpected worlds collided: Bono and Dan Savage, John Wilson and Harry Styles, and David Byrne and Oliva Rodrigo. Joni Mitchell can now vote in the US. Plus, a shout-out to the cool goth working at Double Dare Records in Burien who was blasting Switchblade Symphony on Saturday morning.
This week in Strangerland, l ocal hip-hop group 4ust Collective stopped by the office for another episode of Noise Complaint .

Bono quoted Dan Savage. While a part of me hoped that the quote involved pegging, “fucking first,” or dangers of being in a PUD (Poly Under Duress) relationship, Bono revealed it was Savage’s powerful insight regarding the AIDS crisis that helped inspire U2’s new album, Carnaval De Luz . Bono told the New York Times : “There’s a Dan Savage quote about when he was an AIDS activist in San Francisco in the middle of that crisis. He said: ‘In the morning, we would bury our friends. In the afternoon, we’d go out to protest so we’d have less people to bury. Then, in the evenings, we would go out and dance, because the dance was what we were fighting for.’ I loved that so much. That is not surrendering to the melancholy. That’s the defiance.”

Joni Mitchell can now vote in the US. In an Instagram post shared last Tuesday, Mitchell announced that after a 62-year-long journey, she’s officially become a US citizen. On Thursday, she posted another statement to socials, clarifying to the haters that she became a citizen so that she could vote: “I didn’t give up my Canadian citizenship, and I never will,” she wrote. “I’m a proud Canerican like Neil Young.”

The History of Harry . It was announced this week that documentarian John Wilson (whose new film The History of Concrete has been doing numbers at the box office) has been filming Harry Styles’s 30-night Madison Square Garden residency for an upcoming tour documentary. I think this is a fun idea, and with Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter Live at Carnegie Hall dropping next month, it seems like film auteurs making concert movies is back in style. Next, I’d like to see Werner Herzog direct a Post Malone concert film.

Billy Joel might never perform again. On Thursday, the Piano Man sent a health update to The Hollywood Reporter . “What the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion,” Joel disclosed, adding that he currently isn’t allowed to drive, and won’t know if he can get back on stage or his beloved motorcycles until further testing is done. Joel underwent surgery early last year and canceled his remaining tour dates following a diagnosis of hydrocephalus, a neurological condition that has impacted his balance.

New music incoming: Lana Del Rey joined Zach Bryan on his new song “ Lies .” Blondie announced their first album in nine years. Brother of the dearly departed neo-soul icon D’Angelo confirmed that a posthumous album is on the way. Chappell Roan joined Oliva Rodrigo on her “ Expectations ” remix with a candy-colored music video, complete with a David Byrne cameo, incredible wigs, and Jetsons -style animation.

articles.title: Slog AM: Suspect in Gas Station Murder Captured, Ballard Can Pretty Much Forget About Light Rail, Trump Starts Fraudster Hotline
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: The man suspected of shooting to death an attendant at a Belltown gas station was arrested yesterday in Chicago by US Marshals . The murder happened on October 13 around 5 a.m. and was captured by a surveillance camera. The suspect, Micheal Fleming, is seen entering the gas station, approaching the counter, and shooting the victim, 36-year-old Graeme Dobbeck, four times at close range. Fleming, who had worked at the gas station for four years, was later identified by his former boss as the shooter in the video. Officials also suspect Fleming killed his mother and stepfather at their home in Kenosha, Wisconsin a few days ago.

Ballard keeps getting bad news from Sound Transit. First, $10 billion is needed to reach that part of town . And even if that money is secured, Ballard will not see the opening of a train station until 2042. And if that doesn’t work out, fuck all will happen until 2060. That’s 34 years from now. Many of us, including myself, will be pushing up daisies around that time. But my chances of seeing Link stations open in West Seattle are not that bad. If all goes as planned, they will open in 2035 .

After I’m done with AM , I’ll take a walk through this excellent morning fog. It’s even animated like a ghost that’s silently rubbing its back on the window panes of nearby homes and creeping past and through deciduous trees that are denuding their branches for the long and dark winter. There are few things more haunting than passing a stranger in a fog. Where did they come from? Where are they going? Fog, please wait for me. I will be with you, in you momentarily. Expect a high 61 today.

Let’s consider this for a moment . Manjit Bedi, the 64-year-old former owner of a Tacoma store that, according to Acting US Attorney for the Western District of Washington Neil Floyd, “engaged in fraudulent activity by processing SNAP cards for his own personal benefit, amounting to about $600,000 of taxpayer money…” Bedi bounced right after his indictment in April 2026 and returned to India. He then ended up on the FBI’s “Most Wanted Fraudster” list and was recently captured and extradited. He now faces 20 years in prison.

But how can one find this particular execution of justice at all meaningful when corruption has become the bread and butter of the person who holds our country’s top political office? How are we supposed to applaud the FBI, when rule after rule, law after law is broken for the benefit of a president whose level of corruption is nothing short of mind-boggling? The conversion of “federal assistance dollars into [$600,000 in] cash for personal profit” looks like chicken scratch when compared to the deal that got Julio Herrera Velutini, a Venezuelan billionaire facing felony bribery charges, a pardon.

Why did Donald Trump pardon Julio Herrera Velutini? Because Herrera’s daughter offered Trump’s former attorney, and former senior advisor at the Justice Department, Alina Habba, basically $50 million bucks. That’s it. And this is not some fringe story. It’s in the New York Times . Read all about it . And what was Julio Herrera’s crime? Campaign-finance violation. And keep in mind, this is just one of many such bribes tied to the present administration. “Kimberly Guilfoyle out here begging for $100k to set up meetings while Alina Habba cashing $50M checks,” Bay Area venture capitalist Deva Hazarika posted on X .
Quickly , Wikipedia’s definition of bribery : “It is the corrupt solicitation , payment , or acceptance of a private favor in exchange for official action” Nuff said.

No, not done yet. Shocked by a Fox News poll that found 88 percent of voters placed government corruption at the top of their concerns (above inflation, above gas prices), Trump has set up a Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program (WHIP) that offers citizens up to $30,000 for a tip that results in a fraud conviction. The bizarre thing about this whole shady business is that Trump will personally decide who gets the money or not . “I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions,” Trump said in the Oval Office yesterday. “In other words, I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving.” And who does this arbiter see as deserving? During the WHIP announcement, “Trump honored right-wing influencer Nick Shirley with a $10,000 reward for exposing suspected fraud in Minnesota.”

Enough about corruption. Let’s get some death in the AM. Yes, the end of the world is really right around the corner. New research shows that Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier is going to collapse sooner than initially thought. And this is the “widest glacier in the world.” It’s “roughly the size of Great Britain or the state of Florida.” So when it goes down, much of our world, the human world, the only world we know, will go down with it. This is why it’s called The Doomsday Glacier. We have reached the point of no return. This massive pack of ice is going down no matter what we do: drive electric cars, eat plant-based burgers, tax carbon liberators, and so on. In the words of Private Hudson : “That’s it, man. Game over, man. Game over! What the fuck are we gonna do now? What are we gonna do?”

Let’s end AM with a key track for an October 29 show called See You at The Crossroads , a show about death in hip hop, a show that includes me, Dr. Daudi Abe, and Vitamin D on the ones and twos. The track is “Grand Groove” by Intelligent Hoodlum (Tragedy Khadafi). It’s about “living and dying, about losing people that’s real close to you.”

Jason Molina grew up in a trailer in the working-class city of Lorain, Ohio. The city’s skyline once flickered with blue flames and a warm orange glow emanated from clattering steel mills, but by Molina’s teenage years, Lorain was in a tailspin. “Things were really on the economic decline,” says Tommy Nickoloff, Molina’s childhood friend and director of a new documentary: You Fuckers Figure It Out: A Jason Molina Story. “Nobody had any money and we were encouraged to get out. It’s a place where the American dream was born and died. And we watched it die.”

Molina did indeed get out: the singer-songwriter released almost 20 studio albums and numerous EPs, primarily under the monikers Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co, spanning lo-fi to slowcore via polished Americana and alt-country. By 2009, he estimated he had written thousands of songs. But he died in 2013, aged 39, after years of alcoholism.

articles.title: ‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?
articles.author: Henry Roberts
paras: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?

In You Can See Everything, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency”. Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. “The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”. It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0”, which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says.

That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew?

I popped a disc in my spine a few months back, and one of the things that saved me a lot of pain during my recovery was slip-on shoes .
