articles.title: State Lawmaker, SDOT Director Clash Over Aurora Avenue Overhaul
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Slow progress in advancing plans for the future of Aurora Avenue appears to be leading to mounting tensions between state legislators and the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). Those tensions came to a head in an email exchange just this month between Representative Julia Reed (D-36th LD, Queen Anne) and Acting SDOT Director Angela Brady, a copy of which was obtained by The Urbanist.

The spicy exchange comes more than four years after state lawmakers set aside $50 million for improvements to Seattle's deadliest roadway, which also operates as State Route 99 for its entire length within city limits. An earmark spearheaded by former state Senator Reuven Carlyle, who referred to Aurora as a "scar, ripping through the center of our city", those funds were intended to be a down payment on a fully transformed corridor that he compared to the Champs-Élysées.

But things remain stuck in the planning stage, despite legislative direction in 2022 targeting upgrades between N 90th Street and N 105th Street as a demonstration project that would pave the way for changes elsewhere. SDOT ultimately did not follow that direction, setting up a safety project to look at the entire corridor between South Lake Union and N 145th Street and looping in King County Metro and Seattle Public Utilities in a move that was certain to make the project harder to implement.

Meanwhile, transportation advocates have shifted their focus further south, to the stretch of Aurora Avenue that divides sections of the Fremont neighborhood from each other. Reconnect Fremont, a project of the Aurora Reimagined Coalition (ARC), represents a push for new marked crossings and bus stops that will start to stitch the neighborhood back together. Families with kids at B.F. Day Elementary School who live on the east side of Aurora currently have to use an overpass at N 41st Street to access school, something that doesn't really work for households who get around by bike.
"We want to cut through the endless studies and build momentum through action," ARC stated in a blog post on Reconnecting Fremont earlier this year.

That goal appears to be shared by Rep. Reed, who serves as Vice Chair of the House transportation committee. Following up on an August call that took place with SDOT and staff from Mayor Katie Wilson's office, Rep. Reed wrote to SDOT Director Brady on October 2 – more than a month after that call took place.

"Wanted to check in from our call in August about looking for the City to take action on the highly needed demonstration projects connecting Fremont across Aurora," Reed wrote. She referenced a commitment made during the calll to set up a meeting between ARC and the consultant team currently looking at potential upgrades to Aurora, from the firm Parametrix. "[I]n our call, the Mayor’s office committed to looking at these projects and taking more urgent action to implement them or at least coming up with a plan in the short term – has that happened?"

Brady's response skirted around the issue of near-term improvements along Aurora in Fremont, instead reiterating the work the SDOT already has done to improve safety on the corridor without directly utilizing state funding.

"We share the sense of urgency that Aurora Ave N is in need of improvements now," Brady wrote. "Over the last three years, we have expanded bus lane operations, installed No Turn on Red and Leading Pedestrian Intervals (LPIs), repainted and widened all crosswalks, added center medians and hardened centerlines to reduce turning conflicts, and updated signal timing corridor-wide to increase pedestrian crossing times. We are currently wrapping up construction of a new signal at N 137 th St and completing designs for another package of additional near-term improvements."

But Brady, who took over as Interim SDOT Director in January after a long stint in the city's Office of the Waterfront & Civic Projects, also told Reed that the department has been having a hard time figuring out how to use the $50 million in funding from the 2022 Move Ahead Washington (MAW) transportation package.

"Generally, we have found that the MAW funds have not been easy for SDOT to use for near-term work. They are administered by WSDOT Local Programs similar to a state grant, making them challenging for the City to pivot and use quickly," Brady said. "Seattle is currently exploring various scenarios for sequencing MAW dollars – including near term improvements and a more focused, targeted approach to longer-term improvements. We look forward to discussing those options with you ahead of session."

Reed wrote back visibly frustrated, framing Brady as backing off a promise to set up the direct meeting between ARC and Parametrix, and a commitment to provide concrete next steps on quick build projects that could help to reconnect Fremont.

"I’m sure it is not the city’s intention to go back on its word to a sitting representative and member of the Transportation committee — especially since as we discussed the heart of this problem is a lack of trust in SDOT to administer the state funds effectively," Reed wrote. "I’ve worked in city government a long time so I speak roundabout email as well as anyone. Please do not spray water on my inbox and then try to convince me it is raining."

Reed was even more blunt in an aside in a follow-up email directed to Alex Hudson, at the time Katie Wilson's Senior Policy Advisor on Transportation & Livability. (Hudson has since spent several weeks filling in as Wilson's Interim Press Secretary, but is now returning to her prior role.)

"If the city does not plan to keep the commitments we discussed then I will note that 1) the City is not a trustworthy partner than can be relied on to do what it says it will do when it comes to Transportation work, which will just for the record have an influence on the level of effort I want to put in to advocate for city priorities at the state level and 2) recommend to Chair Fey that the $50 million could be better used in a more directed fashion to improve near term conditions on Aurora," Reed wrote.

Reed, responding to an inquiry about the email exchange via text, made it clear that funding for Aurora remains a priority for her office, but reiterated her frustration with the City of Seattle's pace of action.

"I will say for the record I have no wish to diminish funding for Aurora or to endanger the set aside which goes back to Reuven Carlyle days. But I do want SDOT to take ARC seriously and to take me seriously when I say that waiting two more years before you even think about doing a project is not acceptable," Reed wrote. "This is about trust as much as anything, and following through on the small commitments and pushing forward the bigger demonstration projects is how SDOT builds trust with me and the community that we’re really on the same page."

"Also I commend all the hard work ARC members have put in as volunteers to create a reasonable, achievable, and practical vision," Reed continued. "I don’t think they’re asking for that much and I think city departments should be doing cartwheels of joy to have community members who are so organically engaged at a time when SDOT routinely spends thousands trying to produce even a fraction of this engagement."

Since the email exchange, Reed and Brady met one-on-one this past Friday, a meeting that reportedly went positively. SDOT spokesperson Ethan Bergerson portrayed the department as making progress on Aurora in a statement provided to The Urbanist in the wake of that meeting.

"Acting Director Angela Brady and SDOT staff have a commitment, responsibility, and desire to improve safety on Aurora Ave N. We greatly value Representative Reed’s partnership on this important project and appreciate the work of advocates in continuing to elevate and participate in solutions for the critical needs on Aurora Ave N," Bergerson wrote. "There was a misunderstanding about a commitment made in a meeting regarding the Aurora Ave Project. Now that we’re aware of the misunderstanding, we are scheduling a meeting in November between members of the Aurora Reimagined Coalition and our consultant team."

Bergerson noted that SDOT is working toward wrapping up the planning phase on the Aurora project by next year, a condition of state grant funding the city has already received. $3 million allocated by the legislature remains unobligated, out of the city's reach. Receiving the remaining $44 million will require direct coordination with legislators.

Whether the Aurora project can finally see some forward momentum remains to be seen. And Reed's email exchange voiced concerns that many transportation advocates have raised around the slow pace of work to tackle some of Seattle's most dangerous streets, with the goings-on inside the city's insular transportation department seemingly impenetrable even to a state legislator. Though Mayor Katie Wilson issued an executive order in August directing SDOT to accelerate work on Vision Zero projects, many of the highest-profile corridor overhauls included in the 2024 Seattle Transportation Levy remain in early stages.

"Aurora Avenue is Seattle's most dangerous street. It is polluted, noisy, and divides our neighborhoods. Representative Reed is a strong and steadfast supporter of ARC and our mission to change Aurora for the better. She has worked tirelessly alongside her constituents to ensure SDOT's plan for Aurora is truly transformational," Aurora Reimagined Coalition member Carlo Alcantara told The Urbanist . "Like Rep Reed, ARC would like to see more near-term action on demonstration projects like Reconnect Fremont. These demonstration projects start to reimagine Aurora as a neighborhood main street rather than a highway bisecting our neighborhoods."

articles.title: Lawsuit targets Recology, not city, over deadly 12th and Yesler bike collision — UPDATE
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A tragic death at 12th and Yesler is headed to the courts.

The family of Christian Salyer , the 30-year-old Thurgood Marshall Elementary teacher who died after being struck while riding his bicycle at 12th and Yesler, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit in King County Superior Court against waste contractor Recology and the employee operating the collection truck.
The City of Seattle is not named in the suit despite criticism that officials had scrapped safety improvements in the area where the deadly crash took place.

The legal action stems from the fatal collision on the afternoon of June 1st at the intersection of 12th Ave S and E Yesler Way. According to court documents filed by personal injury firm Panish, Shea, Ravipudi LLP on behalf of Salyer’s estate, parents, and sisters, Salyer was riding southbound in a designated bicycle lane when the Recology driver made an abrupt right turn across the cyclist’s path, striking Salyer and running over him and his bicycle.
Recology has not yet responded to the lawsuit. UPDATE : “Recology cannot comment on pending litigation,” the company said in a statement sent to CHS.

The complaint asserts that video evidence shows that the driver didn’t use his turn signal, “failed to check his mirrors or surroundings, and failed to slow the vehicle before initiating the right turn.”
Beyond alleging operational negligence and traffic code violations, the suit makes claims against Recology for negligent hiring, training, retention, and supervision.

“Recology knew or, in the exercise of reasonable care, should have known that operating a large commercial refuse vehicle creates substantial and foreseeable risks to bicyclists, including when a driver turns across a designated bicycle lane,” the complaint states.

The lawsuit directs its claims at the private waste collection contractor and its employee and does not name the city and the Seattle Department of Transportation as defendants. Fatal bicycle collisions at high-density intersections often lead to liability claims alleging deficient street design, inadequate signal phasing, or visual obstructions. In 2016, the city agreed to a $3.5 million settlement following the 2014 death of cyclist Sher Kung , who was killed by a commercial vehicle turning across an unprotected bike lane on 2nd Ave.

The city has also made more than $6.25 million in combined settlements over cyclist crashes in the past decade along the First Hill Streetcar route that passes through the 12th and Yesler area. The case over Desiree McCloud’s death in 2016 that occurred after a crash on the tracks near 13th and Yesler are included in that total.

When video or physical evidence indicates commercial driver failure, wrongful death actions have bypassed municipal road design claims to pursue corporate carriers and fleet operators directly. The Salyer lawsuit places the blame on Recology.

Across the West Coast, commercial garbage and recycling operators including San Francisco-based Recology have faced scrutiny and wrongful death litigation concerning side-impact visibility, blind spots, and vehicle fleet safety when maneuvering heavy equipment through bicycling corridors.

Similar lawsuits include multi-million-dollar settlements in the Bay Area over fatal right-hook collisions involving cyclists and collection trucks, as well as a $38.8 million Nevada jury verdict against Republic Services after a truck struck a young pedestrian in a crosswalk.

In Seattle, an example is the 2011 wrongful death settlemen t reached on behalf of cyclist Kevin Black , who was killed by a driver making a right turn in a commercial truck in Ballard, as claims centered strictly on the driver’s failure to yield the right-of-way and the commercial operator’s duty to manage turning blind spots.
At 12th and Yesler, meanwhile, the city is taking action.

The intersection has long been identified by transportation advocates as one of Seattle’s most complex transit junctions, characterized by First Hill Streetcar tracks, converging multi-lane arterials, driveway cutouts, and a mix of painted lanes and concrete barriers. Following Salyer’s death, cyclists placed a white ghost bike at the corner during a memorial gathering.

In August , Mayor Katie Wilson remembered Salyer while signing an executive order aimed at accelerating the city’s Vision Zero initiative, directing transportation officials to speed up safety updates on high-collision corridors, including improvements along 12th Ave.

“Seattle should be a city where families can feel safe getting where they need to go — whether they’re walking their kids to school, biking to the park, or taking transit,” Wilson said. “We’ve made important progress, but every serious injury or death on our streets is one too many. We know what makes our streets safer.”

articles.title: $pent Studios settles into E Pike with $10 bins, a papier-mâché jacket, and big plans beyond the racks
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: Hudson Wakefield’s mom was sitting a few feet away, pricing jeans as he explained how all of this started. She’s the reason, really. When he was in elementary school, she’d take him thrifting, and the habit stuck long before fashion did.
“I wasn’t really super big into fashion, but I just loved thrifting and finding stuff for me,” Wakefield, 24, tells CHS.
These days, that habit fills a Capitol HIll storefront.
$pent Studios had been growing underground a few blocks away on 12th Ave and is now in the heart of the party on E Pike, where it replaced a candle bar on the block home to the Comet .

Wakefield figured he was headed toward film in high school. Then the pandemic hit, the free time piled up, and he and his friends were thrifting more than ever. Along the way, he kept finding pieces people had tossed for a hole or a stain that were still too good for the dump. He grabbed his sister’s sewing machine and started patching.
“Sewing, it’s like therapeutic,” he said. He’d like the custom, one-of-one work to someday match the volume of vintage on the floor. Right now, he admits, he’s in business-running mode.

The 12th Ave basement was where $pent grew the most, Wakefield said, with the shop and concerts sharing the same space. But the landlord wanted a single tenant to take over the whole basement, and $pent only occupied two of the roughly 10 rooms. Taking on the rest was out of range.
“We were basically getting kicked out of there, and I got this just in time,” he said. The E Pike spot was the better location anyway.

People will says things are overpriced, no matter what, Wakefield says, even at $5. He points to the $10 bin, where he said you will find jackets that would run $20 to $25 at Goodwill . Sourcing cheaply from thrift stores lets him keep prices down, and he tells people who sell to the shop that he’s offering a fair price, not lowballing them to mark it up tenfold.
“We’re just giving a fair price for us so we can be able to sell it for a good price for the customer, but then also try to be as fair to the person selling as possible,” he said.
The racks are organized by type, with $pent’s own pieces mixed right in. Flip through and you might hit Gucci, then Balenciaga, then a $pent piece, then a random $15 vintage tee.
“You never know what’s next when you’re looking at the rack,” Wakefield said.

Ask him what a first-timer should see, and Wakefield points to what he’s been calling the papier-mâché jacket. It’s not really wearable. It’s more art than clothing, and it came out of a fashion show $pent staged in April with Goodwill at its Dearborn store.

That partnership had an unlikely start. Wakefield and a group of models walked into the Goodwill unannounced and staged a fashion show in the middle of the store while staff were rotating stock. He half expected someone to call the police. Instead, Goodwill told him they didn’t love the lack of permission, but they liked the idea. About six months later, they made it official, with every piece shopped from Goodwill and reworked.
What makes a thrifted find a $pent piece? “I gotta do something to it,” Wakefield said. Sometimes that’s a full rework. Sometimes it’s printing a logo on something that’s already great.

$pent’s old space doubled as an all-ages DIY venue. That won’t work on E Pike, Wakefield said, but pop-ups, meet-and-greets, and small after-parties are still in the plan. Bigger shows will move to venues around the city. The shop’s next fashion show is set for the Comet with DJs, and it’s $pent’s first 21-and-over event. Another collaboration with Neumos across the street is in the works for November.
He still wants to keep putting on for the under-21 crowd. “I know how it is,” he said.

This summer’s Capitol Hill Block Party came with its own lesson. The store was largely fenced off, but organizers gave $pent a free booth inside the grounds. The shop made good money, met a lot of people, and the crew watched the headliner from the front steps. Wakefield hopes to be more involved in coming years.
“I feel like we could be a valuable part of that somehow, more than just popping up,” he said.

$pent is part of a robust thrift, vintage, and consignment community around Capitol Hill including Break Away and Magpie Thrift in the old Red Light space on Broadway. Wakefield puts his shop in the middle of the scale. $pent has sold pieces for as much as $7,000. It also has the $10 bin, and sometimes things go out the door for free.

These blocks of the Pike/Pine nightlife core also have made spaces for a diverse pocket of the fashion economy. Longtimers like Veridis and BAIT are being joined by new projects like the Furesh furry store while Sergius & Bacchus has new energy in a new space in the old Shikorina bakeshop space on E Pike next to Retail Therapy and the Slow Dance vintage and consignment shop. The Out of the Closet thrift shop helps round out the offerings.

Moving to E Pike has meant moving far more volume, so Wakefield is out, sourcing every day. He goes to estate sales and thrift stores, and he has even pulled a few things from abandoned buildings –“a little sketchy,” he said. The best stuff, though, comes from people walking in to sell or trade. A batch of leather jackets is about to hit the floor.

Black Friday sales, more shows, and a fully stocked store, for starters. Longer term, Wakefield wants $pent to be more than a clothing store. He’s thinking furniture, food, and a revival of the $pent energy drinks the brand released in a small run last year. He would also like more real estate in the neighborhood.
“There’s a lot more coming,” Wakefield said.
$pent Studios is now open at 910 E Pike. Learn more at spentstudios.com .

articles.title: Seattle set to pass new rules giving people living in RVs a parking permit — if they accept shelter services
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: (Image: Dee Powers/Center for One Health Research)

Tuesday afternoon, the Seattle City Council is expected to approve a “Vehicle Resident Assistance Program” including a new permit system for people already living in their vehicles, funding for safe lots and secure vehicle storage, and new overnight parking bans across the city. The program will be funded by $5 million already earmarked for homelessness services.
Councilmember Dan Strauss introduced the six-part legislative package this summer.

The cornerstone of the plan is a permitting system for motor homes and travel trailers that is hoped to move more people into more permanent shelter. Eligible vehicle residents identified through a one-time Human Services Department census can obtain a permit allowing overnight parking strictly within designated industrial zones, provided they work with caseworkers and follow neighborhood cleanliness rules. Permits will be revoked if an occupant declines six offers of appropriate shelter.
Unpermitted vehicles would be restricted to two hours of street parking, barred from overnight parking, and subject to immediate impoundment without prior notice.
The permitting and impoundment regulations apply only to “motor homes and travel trailers,” not passenger cars, vans, or SUVs.

Councilmembers are weighing three proposed amendments. Amendment A, sponsored by Councilmember Eddie Lin , would expand the Vehicle Residency Implementation Review Workgroup to include contracted service and outreach providers while broadening its scope to examine warning procedures, equity, and operational readiness. Another proposed Lin amendment directs the workgroup to establish ongoing monitoring metrics, conduct a citywide census of vehicle residents, and deliver annual evaluation reports to the council. Finally, Amendment C, sponsored by Councilmember Maritz Rivera , mandates the revocation of a permit if the holder is convicted of, or enters a diversion agreement for offenses involving drug dealing, sex trafficking, commercial sexual exploitation of children, or prostitution-related loitering.

For unpermitted RVs and trailers, new restrictions taking effect next April will cap street parking at two hours citywide and ban overnight parking between midnight and 6 AM. For the first 90 days, violations will result in a warning. After that, the program will establish impoundment authority.

For passenger cars parked on public streets, standard Seattle Municipal Code rules continue to apply including the general citywide 72-hour maximum parking limit, existing residential/timed parking zones, and standard 24-hour warning notices prior to impoundment.

Supporting ordinances update the Land Use Code for vehicle storage, expand leasing caps to 100,000 square feet for safe lots, modernize the definition of “junk vehicles” to streamline blighted vehicle removal, and fund eight city staffing positions.
Officials say the package is intended to match improved regulation and enforcement with expanded services to help people who live in vehicles of all types in the city.
Approximately 27% of individuals experiencing unsheltered homelessness in King County live in vehicles including cars, vans, buses, RVs, and travel trailers.

Concerns the new Seattle program will push vehicle homelessness outside the city will mean stricter rules across the region. King County Council Vice Chair Reagan Dunn is proposing new regulations for roads and public rights-of-way in unincorporated King County “to prevent Seattle’s homelessness crisis from spilling into neighboring communities.”
UPDATE 7:40 PM : The legislative package was approved. From the announcement:

As with all legislation passed by the Seattle City Council, the VRAP will be presented to the mayor for approval and signature. Once signed, the bills will become effective in 30 days, except for CB 121281, the new regulations on RVs. That law would be scheduled to go into effect April 30, 2027, with a warning period before enforcement officially begins July 31, 2027.

paras: I think I’ve developed a crush on my wife’s ex. I’m in my forties and my wife is older than me. We’ve been together for fifteen years. We are both women. Before we dated each other, we dated men exclusively. She had told me a lot about her ex before me. They were together for six years and lived together, so he came up a lot. I was really insecure at the beginning of our relationship and felt really jealous of him. As time went on, I became more secure in our relationship and I stopped thinking about him. They never spoke while we dated. That is until about two years ago, when he called out of the blue to say he was in town and asked if she wanted to meet up for dinner. We already had dinner plans so I told her to ask him to join us. The dinner was pretty awkward, as you could tell he was nervous. He cried at least once and kept asking us if we were happy in our relationship. He shared that night that he and his wife were in couples counseling for the second time. My initial reaction was to be put off by him and the whole experience — too much sharing — and I could still sense sexual tension between him and my wife. She wants nothing to do with him. However, recently I’ve been thinking about him and have realized I think he’s hot. I know he has a big dick. I would love to sleep with him but I don’t even know what he thinks of me from that one dinner. My wife has always said that I could open up our relationship if I wanted to sleep with someone else. She’s not interested in sleeping with anyone else but would be fine with me doing it as long as we discussed it first. However, I’m not sure she meant that she’d give her blessing for me to sleep with her ex. My questions:
1. What do I even do here? 2. Should I just leave it as a fantasy? 3. Should I bring it up to her? 4. Should I contact him? 5. Have I finally lost my mind?
Thinking Really Intensely About Novel Group Love Experience
1. Keep your mouth shut. 2. Yes, you should. 3. No, you should not. 4. Abso-fucking-lutely not. 5. Sounds like it.

Crushes are a kind of madness, TRIANGLE, and we’ve all been there — we’ve all lost our minds, some of us way more than once. Hell, I don’t think someone who’s never had an obsessive, all-consuming, wildly inappropriate crush can really say they’ve lived. And while it sounds like this crush only recently bubbled up, this guy has loomed large in your psychosexual imagination for a very long time. But just as you’re not the first person to lose their mind like this, you aren’t the first person whose jealousy transubstantiated into lust. (Yes, yes: We see you, aromantic people! You are valid! But even if you’ve never had a mad crush on someone , you’ve surely had a crush on something . Cinnamon rolls? Weighted blankets? Percussion massagers?)

And while it might help this dude to know your relationship isn’t perfect either — his ex’s partner has struggled with obsessive jealousy and now has a crazy-making crush on someone else — I can’t see how it would help him to know he was the focus of your obsessive jealousy and is currently the focus of your obsessive crush. As for the sexual tension you perceived between your wife and her ex, TRIANGLE, that sounds like projection. After all, you’re the one who wants to fuck this guy, not your wife, who says she wants nothing to do with her ex. And, I’m sorry, but there’s no way for you to act on your desire to fuck this guy — which, again, sounds like an eroticized fear — without getting your wife involved.
Luckily for you, TRIANGLE, crushes are almost always a temporary insanity. Like the jealousy that came before it, this too shall pass. Pray on it, masturbate about it, wait it out.

P.S. I’m such a contrarian that I can’t even resist contradicting myself: If you absolutely, positively must bring up the subject of fucking her hung ex with your wife (!), you could claim to have had an erotic dream about her ex and see how she reacts. Try to be neutral, bemused, and matter-of-fact when you mention your dream. (Don’t make the mistake I detailed in my response to Q6 here !) If your wife reacts with horror, drop it forever . If she sighs and says that she sometimes misses the sex and/or that big dick… you could continue to discuss him (maybe have one or two more dreams to goose the convo along) and see where it goes. But follow her lead, TRIANGLE, and be prepared to pivot to praying on it, masturbating about it, and waiting it out.

My 11-year-old granddaughter has discovered masturbation. She is in full-on puberty and she has her period but is very much emotionally a child. She uses the family percussion massager for self-stimulation and keeps it in her bed. No one is particularly concerned about the self-stim, but I am concerned about her use of the massager. It is not delicate stimulation and seems designed for back and shoulder massage. My question is, could it be harmful used on her genitalia? I’m thinking her delicate female parts may end up completely desensitized especially since it is used frequently. My daughter-in-law seems unconcerned and my son steers clear of that topic. What do the experts say?

I’m no expert, TMI, but lots of adults have told me about all the crazy things they used to self-stimulate when they first began exploring their bodies as kids, and almost all report growing up to be sexually healthy adults with fully functional/sensate genitalia. Maybe survivorship bias is at play here — I haven’t spoken to guys who didn’t survive putting their dicks in a vacuum cleaner hoses at age eleven, what with them being dead and all — but I’ve heard so many off-the-wall stories, from men and women alike, and I’ve always asked the obvious follow-up question: “Are you okay now?” (If someone tells me they used the family blender as a sex toy, I’m allowed to ask as many follow-up questions as I want.) And very few reported lasting trauma and/or loss of sensation on account of the banister railings, blenders, rolling pins, washing machines, cucumbers, personal massagers, etc., etc., etc., they experimented with as kids.

But I imagine more would’ve reported lasting trauma if their grandmother had known how they were masturbating and had decided it was her job to intervene. Also potentially traumatizing: their grandmothers writing to sex-advice columnists about the precise stage of puberty they were in (full-on is the most serious stage!), whether they were having periods yet, what the experts might’ve said, etc.

Here’s what you do: Say your piece to her parents — that’s a grandmother’s right — and then slowly disappear into the bushes . Worst-case scenario, your granddaughter grows up to be one of the many adult women out there who need the kind of powerful stimulation only a vibrator can provide in order to climax. Since there’s no way of knowing what percentage of those women conditioned themselves to need those powerful sensations during childhood explorations and what percentage would’ve needed those powerful sensations regardless, TMI, your best course of action is to stay out of it.

P.S. So, it was a woman who confided in me about sneaking into the kitchen at night when she was a teenager and swiping the blender — just the base, not the pitcher — and taking it to her room, where she would plug it in, turn it on high, and press the side of it between her legs over her sweats. Her mother found the blender in her bed on more than one occasion, and never once asked what she was doing with it… because her mother knew. This is anecdote and not data, I realize, but this woman told me she’s fine now, thanks, she doesn’t require a blender in order to come, and her mother eventually left a vibrator — still in the box — under her pillow.

P.P.S. I hope your daughter-in-law is talking to her daughter about sexual health, that she’s already told her know it’s normal for kids her age to explore their own bodies alone and safely and in private, and that your DIL has also told her that, right now, no one else should be touching her body. If she’s done/said all that, your DIL is doing great. Once you’ve verified the above, you could — one last time — express your concerns about your granddaughter using “the family percussion massager” to explore and then add: “Maybe you could leave a gentler gentler ‘personal massager’ on the same shelf where you keep that percussion monster. And now I’ll butt out!”

I’m a bisexual , 28-year-old man in a monogamous relationship with a 26-year-old woman. We’ve been dating for four years. My partner knows I’m bi and is fine with me using solo exploration to get that out, but recently, solo exploration isn’t cutting it anymore. I feel a very strong urge to be with a man again that at times verges on overpowering. My partner is not comfortable with an open relationship of any kind. I don’t want to cheat and lose a good relationship, but I’m also not sure how long I can hold out against these urges. Any advice is greatly appreciated!

paras: Our corporate overlords don’t oppose the Millionaires Tax: Or at least, they aren’t spending big to destroy it at the ballot, as they have done to similar income tax proposals in the past, the Seattle Times reports . The lack of oligarch backing means the petite bourgeois small business tyrants must fund the repeal on their own, and they’re being outspent by the big unions. I’ll have more on the why later, but in short, Washington’s major corporations can read the writing on the wall, and know that if we fail to tax the income of millionaires the progressive taxation movement will expand corporate taxation instead. And shifting your tax burden onto someone else is what tax reform is all about.

Prosecutor in Washington’s second-largest city reopens investigation into deadly police shooting after reporting by local media: You can tell it’s an election year because Spokane County’s incumbent prosecutor has reopened an investigation he closed two months ago into local cops who fatally shot a local man. The announcement comes only a few weeks after Spokane-based news outlet RANGE published texts from the officers, such as “So what’s the crime we were investigating yesterday? Unlawful discharge? Haha.”

The WNBA trans panic is a fake campaign amplified by a small network of money-grubbing influencers and pundits: Data analytics company GUDEA analyzed hundreds of thousands of posts on the subject over the summer, and found that only eight of them gained significant traction, and were pushed by influencers trying to make money. “If you take out the eight top posts, this [narrative] didn’t happen. Nobody would be talking about this,” GUDEA told Rolling Stone . So if you believe this nonsense, it is not an original thought—you were programmed by a machine, you live in The Matrix. I’m trying to free your mind, but I can only show you the door.

The WNBA might remain the only game in town for Seattle basketball fans: ESPN and the Seattle Times report the NBA expansion cabal has placed our fair city on the backburner once again, which is why you don’t get your hopes up about the return of a team named after vaporware that failed so spectacularly that it crashed the local economy and documentarians started making films about local child poverty.

Longview Daily News is the latest Washington paper we’re highlighting for trying to replace journalism with AI bullshit: The paper in owned by Lee Enterprises, one of the smaller of the bad national chains of local newspapers, and which you probably haven’t heard of unless you’re from Montana, where they own nearly every major metro daily, or what’s left of them after laying off almost the entire state press corps and selling their printers and buildings for cash. Lee Enterprises’ latest suicidal moneymaking scheme is publishing AI deepfakes and refusing to give their workers contract guarantees that they won’t be replaced by poorly-programmed machines. The Longview NewsGuild (part of the same labor union that reps Stranger workers, by the way) has been bargaining since July to get management to please just act like a normal newspaper.

They should have sent a cowboy: Klickitat County Sheriff Bob Songer is one of those libertarian LARPers who thinks they are the highest law of the land and make it everyone else’s problem. The “constitutional” sheriff, infamous for his literal posse, is retiring, and his potential successors are mulling how many of his far-right traditions they should echo to attract voters this election, Investigate West reports .

Why did we ever believe the Yakima grifter behind the world’s most famous Bigfoot footage? If you’re ever tracking a Sasquatch in Klickitat County and worried that bagging it across the county line will expose you to Skamania County’s fascist Bigfoot conservation ordinance, I have good news: Bigfoot is not real. Marq Evans’ new documentary Capturing Bigfoot exposes Washington man Roger Patterson’s famous Klamath River footage as fake by interrogating the man’s life as a stereotypical Pacific Northwest conman, Variety reports .

Hitler News: Declassified report shows CIA resettled Nazis in Canada: If you are an avid Tuesday morning Slog AM reader then you have been waiting with breath as bated as mine for the release of the “Rodal Report” after the Canadian judiciary cleared the investigation into how so many Nazis ended up in their country for publication earlier this year. “Nazi War Criminals in Canada: The Historical and Policy Setting from the 1940s to the Present,” as the report is officially known, was created in the 1980s when the Canadian government was forced to publicly investigate their Nazi problem, ending with a massive coverup. Read details of the CIA’s rat lines to Canada in the Maple .

US-backed Alberta referendum fails: Transplanting a bunch of Nazis into Canada wasn’t the end of US interference with our neighbors to the north. Alberta has long been the farthest right member of the confederation, evidenced by—what else—one of those aforementioned resettled Nazis becoming the president of the province’s long-ruling Tory party. It’s always been the most American-inflected province, too, due to high US immigration, as well as the influence of the Houston-based oil industry that runs the place the way Marco Rubio runs Venezuela from Mar-a-Lago. If the whole “a Nazi leads our ruling party” didn’t make the reality of Conservative rule in Alberta clear enough, leaders supporting the local independence movement to spite the Liberal prime minister (in the most charitable read) should tell you how serious these people are about providing for their constituents.

I thought Lance Oppenheim was the same guy as Joshua Oppenheimer, which means my expectations going into You Can See Everything were a bit off. I figured Nathan Fielder’s turn from comedic rehearsal to dark reenactment must have been influenced by Oppenheimer’s use of reenactment to interrogate the perpetrators of the Indonesian genocide of communists and Chinese in 1965-66 in his documentary The Act of Killing. But this is not true, because Oppenheim is not Oppenheimer, and I am a fool. articles.title: Housing Accountability Act Puts Tiny Beaux Arts Village in the Spotlight
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Changes to state law intended to broaden access to more affordable types of housing are reverberating in some unexpected places, including within Puget Sound's smallest jurisdictions. Last week, the town council in Beaux Arts Village – population 310 – met to approve a slate of temporary zoning changes, under threat of state sanctions and prompted by the 2025 Housing Accountability Act. While the vote was unanimous, the meeting included plenty of hand-wringing about the path the town had taken to get to that point.

Clocking in at just 0.17 square miles, Beaux Arts Village is a town entirely ensconced within the City of Bellevue, a pocket of narrow, tree-lined streets where golf carts are more commonplace than apartment buildings. Founded in 1908 as an artist's colony, the town's initial boosters drew residents with advertisements in the Seattle Times touting the fledgling community as "an expedition into the realms of Utopia." The town's primary amenity is a 1,100 foot stretch of beach, which only town property owners have access to as members of a separate, non-profit organization known as the Western Academy of Beaux Arts.

In 1954, Beaux Arts officially incorporated, to "protect the beach and the Village lifestyle," according to the town's website today. It had taken two years for Beaux Arts to reach the required 300-resident minimum necessary to be able to become a town, but just over seven decades later the population has only changed by six residents. Today, the median home value in Beaux Arts Village is $2.6 million.

In the decades since the implementation of Washington's 1990 Growth Management Act (GMA), the state-mandated growth plans in enclaves like Beaux Arts Village haven't traditionally been subjected to much scrutiny. But in 2025, the state legislature passed the Housing Accountability Act , empowering the Washington Department of Commerce to directly evaluate whether local jurisdictions are meeting the expectations laid out in state law when it comes to accommodating housing. Before that law was approved, the only avenue for a local Comprehensive Plan to be found inadequate was through a citizen appeal – though the state has sometimes taken the drastic step of making that appeal itself in extreme circumstances.

In January, Commerce announced that Beaux Arts Village had been selected as one of the first eight jurisdictions ever subjected to "selected review" under the Housing Accountability Act. As part of that review, agency staff have been tasked with determining whether all eight are in compliance with all aspects of the GMA, including new provisions that direct localities to plan for housing across different income levels – requirements that many cities have found vexing.

Beaux Arts' 2024 Comprehensive Plan was reviewed with a fine-toothed comb, and in June a preliminary report was issued to town officials that listed everything that needed to be adjusted to get into alignment with state law, in Commerce's view. That letter gave town officials their marching orders, and started the clock.

"We've been at it for nine months. We presented a Comp Plan that I think is in alignment with what everybody here will believe is keeping with what the village is, which has been much like the past three or four Comp Plans that we put together," Beaux Arts Councilmember Tom Stowe said Tuesday. "Commerce came in and shredded it, basically, and said that we couldn't do what we basically wanted."

Beaux Arts Village's share of Puget Sound's expected housing growth over the coming decades is not substantial. In fact, when King County handed out housing growth targets across all 39 cities and towns countywide in 2021 – an expectation of the number of new units to plan for through 2044 – the number was just one. Its neighbor Bellevue is planning for 35,000.

And yet the town's existing land use, intended to preserve a "tranquil, calm living environment" per the current Beaux Arts Village Comprehensive Plan, has presented certain challenges when it comes to growth plan compliance. Per a 2021 adjustment to the GMA known as House Bill 1220, Beaux Arts Village is required to plan for that one housing unit to be occupied by a household making 30% of King County's median area income or below – households that overall have the greatest difficulty finding housing.

30% of King County's median income is just under $40,000 for a family of two, and residents bringing in that little income cannot afford the single family homes that make up the vast majority of the town's housing stock, nor can they afford the backyard cottages that are allowed on those lots either.

To make it feasible to build at least one home that could be within reach to that future low-income household, Commerce recommended that Beaux Arts Village officials adjust zoning to allow some type of multifamily housing within their borders. Beaux Arts ultimately settled on the idea of creating a co-living "overlay." Co-living housing, also referred to as single-room occupancy (SRO) homes, provide the lowest rents even when built without any subsidy.

Though the idea of allowing six units of co-living housing just on one block of Beaux Arts Village was considered by the town planning commission, but counting on six property owners to build that specific type of housing would likely fall short of providing the necessary capacity. Instead, a proposal advanced that would allow co-living housing outside of the town's "erosion control hazard area" closest to Lake Washington.

The Beaux Arts Village planning commission deadlocked 2-2 on the idea of scaling back Commerce's recommendation to allow six co-living units on all lots in the overlay, but the town council ultimately did scale that number back to four. The fewer units allowed in the overlay, the less likely that it is that any actual co-living projects will get built – an outcome that did come up Tuesday.
"If we think this is about somebody coming in and building, nobody is going to build this," Councilmember Stacy Saal said.

As a town of its size, there is no Beaux Arts Village town hall – just a town mailbox. Town council meetings take place in a rotating councilmember's home, which is how a dining room and adjoining kitchen was transformed into a public meeting room last week for the monthly town council. Twenty to thirty Beaux Arts residents packed into the space, standing in the hallway or sitting on the floor as their elected representatives debated town matters, including whether to get in compliance with state housing law.

The big incentive for councilmembers to act and adopt the interim ordinance, which will expire February 4, was the stick included in the Housing Accountability Act. In addition to being disqualified for some state grants, cities and towns deemed to be out of compliance with the GMA trigger what is known as the Builder's Remedy .

A brand new provision in state law, the Builder's Remedy requires the approval of any complete building permit – no matter whether the underlying project conflicts with the underlying zoning for the site, as long as certain requirements for on-site affordable units are met. Theoretically, this could lead to a ten story apartment building in Beaux Arts Village, as long as a subset of the new units are kept within certain rents.

"If we don't do this tonight, as you all remember, the consequence is we go out of compliance, and the low income builder remedy kicks in, and any low income builder comes in and can submit plans that totally ignore our zoning code, they can come in and build whatever they want," Beaux Arts Mayor Aletha Howes the crowd in attendance on Tuesday. "The only thing they have to follow is setbacks and tree code. Everything else is blown out of water."

So far no jurisdiction has actually triggered the Builder's Remedy, with Carnation getting fully into compliance earlier this summer, and Bainbridge Island going the same route as Beaux Arts and approving a temporary ordinance a few days after Carnation. But in Beaux Arts just as there was on Bainbridge Island, some voices pushed for a more oppositional stance against state review.
During Tuesday's public hearing, local resident Dan Bridges urged councilmembers to take a more adversarial position.

"Well-meaning councils and boards sometimes lose sight of the fact that public agencies, state agencies – who we trust, like our parents, right? – they're still political agencies, and they have an agenda and they have a point of view. That point of view is not always the correct point of view," Bridges said. "Having an outside [entity] of coming to advocate for us would be helpful. And I would suggest if you haven't done that yet, you might consider doing that and not simply accept what some state agency is telling you. Only a judge is the one who decides the law."
For now at least, Beaux Arts Village has deemed the path of least resistance to be compliance.

"It is not that we are not receptive of what we're hearing," Stowe told public commenters. "It's that we quite frankly are up against them to comply, or they're going to go over us and say you have no authority and allow whatever zoning or buildings they say under the code – under Commerce's interpretation of the code, which has not necessarily been ours – and we have pointed that out that we don't read the law the same way they do."
As one of the first jurisdictions being put under the Housing Accountability Act microscope, Beaux Arts officials expressed clear frustration at the process of state review over the past few months.

They're not alone in that frustration. When members of the Carnation City Council held a public hearing with the Department of Commerce in July, many of the same concerns raised in Beaux Arts surfaced – about staff time, not an insignificant issue for a small city or town, and confusion over the purpose of the new law.

"Is this supposed to be helpful for us?," Carnation deputy Mayor Jessica Merizan asked Commerce staff at that July 9 meeting. "Because it really seems like you've pulled a lot of staff time, and the point seems to be saving staff time because these types of errors are happening. It just kind of feels like this is a teacher double-checking work, and not necessarily, these are areas of the community, in the region that perhaps need support, and we're here to offer that."

In Beaux Arts Village, Howes directly referred to what the Commerce department had been tasked with doing as "overreach" and called the idea of the state forcing local officials to spend scarce staff time on that review as an "unfunded mandate" that she called "bullshit."

"I am still pursuing the legislative changes in the next session with [Representative] Zahn, [Representative Thai], and [the Association of Washington Cities] is still pushing the seven legal arguments that we brought to them, and the seven other cities are also pushing to get those changes," Howes said, noting the temporary ordinance's four-month duration. "So if something moves during that time frame, then we can amend. If something doesn't move and it goes to final...you know, we'll see how the legislative session goes in '27."

Meanwhile, five additional cities and towns – including Woodway, Darrington, Gold Bar, Brier, and DuPont – are still in the process of coming into compliance, work that was spurred on by the Housing Accountability Act. And then next year, a whole new slate of jurisdictions will be announced.

articles.title: The AI Wars Come to Ravenna
articles.author: Harry Cheadle
paras: It seems likely that 2026 will be known as the year that AI broke through and became a mainstream political issue. Protests against data centers have swept the country , AI agents are launching cyberattacks against their own kind, and former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon became an overnight celebrity after quitting and warning the public that the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” AI is also worming its way into seemingly every facet of everyday life, from restaurant ads to social media to online dating . Depending on who you ask, the technology could make white-collar labor obsolete, usher in a kind of golden age, be more important than fire or electricity, or turn all humans into paperclips. It’s also central to a state legislative race in North Seattle.

Perhaps you’ve seen the paper ads stapled to telephone poles in North Seattle portraying a tiny person being menaced by a giant robot. “ANXIOUS ABOUT AI?” it asks. “Have you been waiting for someone to do something about it? DON’T WAIT ANY LONGER.”

This is an ad for Will Dreher, who is challenging longtime incumbent Representative Gerry Pollet in the 46th Legislative District, which encompasses North Seattle. Though there have been plenty of races in Seattle and elsewhere featuring a fiery progressive running against a more moderate incumbent, this isn’t one of those races. Pollet is generally regarded as a fairly left-wing legislator (though urbanists oppose his views on housing ). Rather, Dreher is running primarily because he doesn’t think the Washington State Legislature has moved quickly enough to regulate AI.

Dreher is a Harvard Law School grad who clerked for then-future Supreme Court justices Elena Kagan and Brett Kavanaugh. (The latter posting has become controversial in the election, with Dreher saying he didn’t get to choose who he clerked for; he denounced the conservative Kavanaugh after the judge was accused of sexual assault.) In 2019, he moved to Seattle and became a federal prosecutor, volunteering to work on the January 6 insurrection cases. But at the same time, he was reading about AI development and began to regard the technology as “on par with the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons,” he says. Dreher thought pushing back against AI was more important than his work as a prosecutor, which helped motivate him to join the law firm Keller Rohrback, where he’s helping sue Apple’s AI business on behalf of authors who claim their copyrights have been violated.

Dreher doesn’t have many pointed critiques of Pollet in particular (he’s praised Pollet’s work on education funding ), but thinks the Washington State Legislature as a whole has been slow to regulate AI. Lawmakers should have already passed legislation holding AI companies liable for untoward uses of their products, he argues, pointing to deepfake porn of minors as a particularly nasty application of the technology. He also wants the state to make it clear AI won’t replace certain government employees, like teachers, and enact job-protection measures more broadly. Other states like California and New York, Dreher points out, have passed a lot more AI-related bills, including some that try to address the “catastrophic risk” of the technology.
Pollet describes Dreher as a relative neophyte who is new to both the district and Washington politics writ large. “Will Dreher has never been involved for a minute in legislation,” Pollet says.

Despite his lack of experience, Dreher’s candidacy has caught the attention of people in the AI industry who would like the technology to be better regulated, and as a result, money has poured into his campaign—he’s raised over $304,000, compared to $214,000 for Pollet. Nearly 83 percent of Pollet’s donations come from in-state contributors, compared to just 20 percent for Dreher. As of publication time, about 36 percent of Dreher’s contributions, or over $112,000, come from people in the AI field, including researchers, engineers, and PhD students who have money to throw around and want to support pro-regulation candidates, even if those candidates are in low-profile races.

This is a trend nationwide, with cash-flush AI workers willing to fund obscure races in the name of pushing for greater AI regulation. OpenAI employees are even contributing to a PAC that is countering their executives’ spending. Individuals at these companies and others have funneled cash into a New York assembly race, a California Senate election, and a bid for governor of Alaska. All of those candidates have promoted strict AI regulations. This same dynamic is funneling money to Dreher.

“Will understands that the current AI regulatory regime is woefully inadequate, and that the largest AI companies need to be held to strong safety standards, to ensure that their products don’t pose a risk of catastrophic harm,” one of these out-of-state donors told The Stranger . “Many of my friends who work at AI companies are worried about existential risk from AI and have told me that they want their companies to be much more regulated, so that those risks don’t materialize. So, after chatting with Will, I decided to donate, and I encouraged some of my friends at AI companies to donate, too.”

The politics around AI regulation can get a little murky. Ian Mosher, the founder of a group called Ethical Tech Washington, says that some people concerned about AI are worried it could kill everyone, but others (including himself) view AI as a more normal technology that should be subject to a normal amount of government oversight. “This is a product that needs to have features that people need, that needs to be safe, that needs to be done in a way that is in alignment with our society,” Mosher says. “The people who are creating it need to be responsible stewards of that technology.”

Mosher recently wrote an op-ed for the Seattle Times that declared that “Washington is behind in the regulation of AI” and argued that the Legislature should pass bills ensuring AI companies would be liable for crimes committed by their systems and that these companies must get licenses to content used to train AIs. “Number of bills isn’t necessarily the best measure” for how well a state is regulating AI, Mosher told The Stranger . What he wants to see is “foundational AI legislation” that can protect consumers and the public from all sorts of potential harms. In his op-ed, he called for the Legislature to pass the People’s Privacy Act, first introduced in the State House in 2021, which would require companies to get opt-in permission from users to get access to their data. If that legislation was in place, he argues, it would be harder for corporations to create aggressive AI tools that take advantage of that data to, for example, set grocery store prices that vary by customer (a practice that just got banned in Seattle). Mosher isn’t endorsing either candidate in the 46th.

Pollet is no defender of the AI industry. He sponsored a bill regulating chatbots that passed this year . He’s also been a sponsor of the People’s Privacy Act, and blames opposition from the tech industry, which favors a weaker form of privacy protections (which he calls a “deepfake”), for its failure to pass. He also supports a moratorium on data center construction—as does Dreher and seemingly every other Democrat in town—and says he’s working with legislators in Oregon on an ambitious two-state proposal that would tax data centers in order to create a fund to help offset impacts from AI-related job losses. Oregon and Washington need to partner on this, he says, because “if you tax on one side of the [Columbia] River, they’ll just put the data center on the other side of the Columbia and get their electricity from across the river.” The Legislature hasn’t been ignoring AI issues, Pollet argues—the state just came out with a task force report recommending a slew of regulations, bills are being worked on, and progress is being made.

Win or lose, Dreher will likely give Pollet one of his toughest races since he took office in 2011. He typically wins with over 80 percent of the vote, but got 52 percent in the primary this summer, with Dreher claiming 31 percent and a third candidate, Ron Davis, earning 16. (Davis has since endorsed Pollet.) Pollet claims that Dreher’s AI industry donors will push him to back off taxing data centers. “When you’re funded by AI, and out-of-state people at that, they’re going to have access to you, that’s a reason for concern,” Pollet says. Dreher says that he has always supported a moratorium on data centers and that his AI-linked donors “have publicly called for many other regulations that would likewise hurt their companies’ bottom lines, like slowing or stopping AI development… So I have no reason to believe they oppose a data center moratorium.”

But whoever ends up representing the 46th, AI is going to loom over them—and everyone else in the Legislature. With the federal government’s unwillingness to regulate the new technology, tech-centric states like Washington have to step up.

“We have the opportunity to do things here in Washington,” says Mosher, with a legislature and governor’s mansion both controlled by Democrats who will have some motivation to address AI. “We have the right kind of constituency, the right kind of people to do it.”

articles.title: Sunday Movie: Service-Led Planning in California Rail
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: In 2004 California released an excellent service-led plan to expand its state rail network, both the high-speed rail projects and other corridors and a few BRT connectors. This video by nandert goes in-depth on why service-led planning is an important paradigm all agencies should use (5:33), the benefits of California’s plan, and how the governing boards would need major structural changes and reforming their priorities to actually make it happen this well.

He defines service-led planning as “Start by determining where the transit demand and need is, and tailor the plan to meet that demand.” In other words, determining how much of what kind of service each corridor needs. Then draw up cost estimates for the resulting lines to operators (agencies). The California plan specifies the rail/bus mode and frequency, but you could also leave the mode for a later step before assigning them to agencies, as Jarrett Walker does.

The difference between this and most transit planning is, corridors are chosen to meet the bulk of mobility/trip needs, without certain city/county jurisdictions having undue influence to override these for demands that contradict them. It also puts frequency first in the spec rather than leaving is as an afterthought, so the public can see what minimum frequency the entire network or each project will have so that they can see what their experience will be like.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Bremerton Should Fully Pedestrianize Quincy Square
articles.author: Travis Merrigan
paras: The City of Bremerton is debating how to use the newly completed, $4 million Quincy Square, located at the heart of downtown. As with Seattle’s Pike Place Market, Bremerton Public Works proposed closing the ‘Q Square’ about half the days of the year. At a Sept 3rd City Council meeting, councilors were split 3-to-3 between supporting the 182-day closure and seeking more car-access days. It’s just the latest debate in an on-going tug of war as the city tries to carve out safe multimodal spaces from Bremerton’s thoroughly car-dominated streets and neighborhoods.

Completed in 2025, Quincy Square is a half-block of 4th Street in the heart of downtown. It features a permanent stage, seating and tables, and interactive music installations honoring the late, great music impresario Quincy Jones, who spent his middle school years in Bremerton, before moving to Seattle.

Q Square was designed as a hybrid street, transforming via mid-block, removable bollards between pedestrian-oriented plaza and a one-way street with 14 parking spots. The debate this fall at Bremerton City Council is about how many days the plaza should be open to cars.

The Public Works plan attempts to split the baby, via middle-of-the-road Resolution No. 3417. The resolution would change Bremerton city code to create ‘pedestrian mall’, under a little used Washington state law from the 1960s. On September 3, City Council voted 5-1 to create a pedestrian mall, but a major rift formed over whether Q Square should be primarily a pedestrian street closed to cars or just a regular street which closes sometimes for events.

Public Works’ initial proposal offered a vision of Quincy Square offering economic, safety and social benefits of a predictable schedule and community gathering space. It also cited the costs of the current, on-again off-again street closures, including resource drain and overtime required to replace signage and bollards at odd hours. The administration’s plan also cited confused drivers, forced into awkward u-turns on a street that might be open the day before.

Public Works is seeking guidance on a separate, administrative decision, to set the calendar which designates which days Q Square is open to traffic. The initial proposal was for about 182 days closed, concentrated in the summer and between Thanksgiving and New Years, with the plaza open to traffic the other 183 days.

During its September 3rd deliberations, Council was split 3-3 (with one councilmember absent) between closing Q Square to cars for at least 182-days per year, and three councilors who sought more car-access days.

Opponents of more pedestrianization of Q Square have understandable and sincere concerns about the downsides of closing the street. People who park or drive on the street are being asked to shoulder a disproportionate burden of an amenity that benefits the entire city.
Those opposing more pedestrianization of Q Square have three primary complaints:

Every multimodal project that restricts automobile access faces backlash from those who would otherwise have unfettered usage of a given space. Q Square is home to four dozen businesses, including a theater, corner store, skate shop and over 30 professional offices in a mid-rise tower. For those people, it’s more convenient to get dropped off right in front of the door than walk from a parking garage or street parking 200 feet away.

And opponents argue that, with the exception of City-sponsored events, the Square is little-used. That too few people - or the wrong kinds of people (e.g., unhoused) - hang out in the Square to justify the loss of parking and car traffic. This echoes a common criticism of ‘empty’ bike lanes; if somebody isn’t constantly in them, the space should be available for cars.

Bremerton must decide if the creation of a central, community gathering space is worth forcing inconvenience on a few dozen drivers every day. This half block of 4th St is probably downtown’s lowest-traffic street, and the 14 parking stalls are just 0.2% of downtown’s 6,300 public parking spaces. And many city amenities - parks, free street parking, park benches, and schools - sit empty most hours of the year. These amenities are valuable because they are available when needed. Nobody tears down a church because it’s empty on a Tuesday afternoon.

The status quo of random 4th Street closures leads to confused motorists making awkward half-block u-turns on a street not fit for purpose. The street could be reconfigured as a u-shaped drop-off site for cars and shuttle buses, with short-term, off-hour parking for deliveries. Resolution 3417 allows acquisition of right of way, and the affected hotel would likely welcome an improvement to the chaotic turn-arounds.

Leaving Q Square closed for long blocks of time allows drivers and businesses to adjust and find new hacks to efficiently navigate and do commerce downtown. Meanwhile, designating Q Square for pedestrians will, over time, attract more people downtown, and delight visitors who stumble across the open space.

Great cities have great plazas. Plazas are where poems are written, friends meet for lunch and kids first learn to ride bikes. The $4 million Quincy Square is brand new and, if left open for people to gather, will become the beating heart of thriving downtown Bremerton. Q Square will help downtown recover from the suburban flight of the 80s and 90s which pulled commerce out of the city, off to distant strip malls outside the city.

In modern-day Bremerton, virtually every inch of downtown street is maximized for vehicles. Among downtown’s 6,300 public parking spots are four, city-owned, multistory parking garages. Most downtown streets host two-way traffic plus dual-side on-street parking. Pedestrians are shunted aside onto narrow sidewalks, with few benches to sit on or places to linger. Street eateries that granted street life to downtown during the pandemic are nearly all swept away, to make room for street parking. The nearest playground swing is 0.75 miles away.

Revitalization of downtown requires people to get out of their cars, window shop and spend money in downtown businesses. A lovely, welcoming square that encourages people to linger will benefit many businesses downtown, even if the lost parking affects some more than others.

Bremerton could take action to reduce the hyperlocal problems caused by vehicle restrictions. Additional short-term and ADA parking could be created very near Q Square. The City could designate the four Pacific Avenue parking stalls nearest Q Square as ADA and place 2-hour parking limits on the bottom two floors of its 4th and Washington parking garage. Also, an improved turn-around and drop-off spot could be created in collaboration with the hotel immediately east of the half-block vehicle barriers.

More people would use Q Square if the city offered very low-cost rental of the space for bike polo matches, band rehearsals and mass outdoor Dungeons and Dragons tournaments (Bremerton’s nerd game is strong). The burden of filling the square need not fall on the City funding big events.

Opponents of closing Q Square predict terrible outcomes. But outcomes will probably be less dire than they predict, especially if Bremerton makes adjustments. Besides, unexpected upsides are just as likely as miserable downsides. Cities have always thrived because of spontaneous interaction in public places, which sparks ideas, creates new commerce and builds community. Q Square is unique in all of Bremerton, but common across the world: a safe, inviting, central plaza where people go just because, and where interesting and unexpected things can happen.
Great cities have great plazas. Quincy Square is Bremerton’s once-in-a-generation shot to create Bremerton’s first great plaza. Let’s not throw away our shot.
The Bremerton City Council will debate the Mayor’s proposal at an upcoming council meeting this fall.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Two RapidRide R Line Stops Restored
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On Wednesday, King County Executive Girmay Zahilay transmitted RapidRide R Line alignment legislation to the King County Council. The R Line will travel between Rainier Beach station and downtown Seattle on Rainier Ave when it opens in 2032. In August, Metro asked the public for feedback on an initial alignment proposal . While many support the project, the planned removal of several existing Route 7 stops drew widespread criticism from Rainier Valley residents , transit advocates , and disability advocates .

In response to this feedback, the latest plan restores the stops on Rainier at Bayview St and State St/Grand St. The King County Council will discuss and vote on the R Line’s alignment over the next few weeks. This will establish the route’s path and general station locations. Additional project components, such as transit priority infrastructure, new crossings, and sidewalk improvements, will be finalized in later project stages. Executive Zahilay has proposed front-loading the project’s budget in an effort to potentially move up the R Line’s opening date.

Another key feedback theme Metro received involved the removal of stops along the Prentice Street loop. Today, every third Route 7 bus continues south of Henderson St to provide coverage in Rainier Beach. The R Line will turn right on to Henderson and terminate at the Rainier Beach Link station. In response, Metro highlighted Route 106 on Renton Ave and the Rainier Beach Metro Flex zone. The agency is also planning a southeast Seattle restructure that will take place in 2028 or 2029. Based on feedback received during restructure process, Metro may adjust other routes to back-fill Prentice St loop coverage once the R Line launches in 2032.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Seattle’s University District
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. So, here’s a short list to get you started.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
